INDIANA AND ILLINOIS NEWS
Elkhart Excited Over a Confession by One of the Men Engaged in a Murder.
Alleged "White Caps" on Trial in Decatur County—Man Suffocated in a Brush Fire— Killed by a Train—Notes and Gleanings.
INDIANA.
A Murderer Confesses His Crime and Implicates Two Other Men.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.
ELKHART, April 27.—In early spring a prominent young colored man, named, Aiken, disappeared one night, after attending a ball, and was supposed to have been murdered by three young men with whom he had trouble at the dance; but the closest search failed to discover the body, and the young men who had been arrested were discharged. To-day one of them, Wilson, confessed that he and the two others had killed Aiken, secreted the body two days in a haystack. and then, tying a heavy weight to it, threw it into Shavehead lake. The men have been arrested, and the lake is being dragged.

ONE OF THREE COLORED MURDERERS COULD NOT KEEP HIS HIDEOUS SECRET.

ELKHART, IND., April 30.—About three months ago, one Friday night, a prominent young colored man named Aiken disappeared after attending a dance, and three young colored men with whom he had some difficulty were suspected of murdering him, but the body could not be found and the crime could not be proved. Unable longer to stand his part in the crime, one of them (Wilson) yesterday confessed his part in the matter, stating that he and the others had murdered Aiken and hidden the body two days, and then, attaching a heavy weight to the body, thrown it into Shavehead Lake. The young men have been arrested, and lynching feeling runs very high.

A MURDER MYSTERY
A MISSING MAN'S BODY FOUND.
Disclosures Concerning a Case County Crime-A Lake Gives Up Its Dead Killed by a Horse Other State News.
VANDALIA, May 4.—On the 23d of last December, John Aikens, a colored man living in Calvin township, Cass county—a township that is largely inhabited by colored people—mysteriously disappeared. He had attended a shooting match, and was very drunk when he started home. At the house of one Gus Harris he drank some more, and since then has not been seen.

Stories were told of an altercation that was heard near the shore of Shave Head Lake, in which Aikens' voice was identified and it has been generally believed that he was murdered and the body put into the lake. Color was given to this idea later, by the statements of a young colored man named Lewis Wilson, who said Harris did the killing, and that the deed was done at or near the Harris house, and that he and Harris put the body into the lake. Wilson was held by the officers to await further developments, but escaped Wednesday. He has been recaptured and is now in jail, as is also Gus Harris, who was arrested on strong suspicion some time ago.

Yesterday, however, Wilson's story was confirmed in part. When the body of Aikens was found in the lake near the house of Alexander Aikens by two fishermen. It was taken to Alexander's house and an inquest begun. There were marks of a heavy blow on the neck, one behind the ear, and the forehead was crushed.

Last Sunday when divers were at work on the lake in search of Aikens' body over 1,500 people were gathered there.

Aikens was 28 years of age and of good parentage, and was very popular in the Long Lake region and other parts of the township.

Wilson claims that Harris and himself took Aikens' body from the barn where Harris put it after the murder, and, conveying it to Shave Head Lake, they weighted it down with a bag of sand securely, as they supposed. Wilson says Harris insisted that his stepmother, who was an old flame of Aikens', had tried to kill Aikens by poison in his drink the day of the murder. This portion of Wilson's story dovetails in with other facts the officers know. Other arrests are expected, and it is believed that as many as many as five persons are directly interested and equally guilty.
aiken-elkhart-1888-03.A5:
Murdered Man's Body Found.
ELKHART, May 4.—The body of John Aikens, the young farmer whose supposed murder, a few miles south of here, in January, created a great deal of excitement, and concerning which young Wilson made a confession, has been found floating in Long lake, with neck broken and the head crushed. The body has on the overcoat in which he was clad the night he was killed. Wilson, in his confession, stated that he was compelled to assist Harris in disposing of the body after the latter had committed the crime, but his statement is supposed to have been made for the purpose of diverting the suspicion which attached to him. Wilson and Harris are held for the crime.

How a Sheriff Outdid Lynchers.

Amos Miller, a Negro, Assaults a White Lady in Maury County.

He is Captured After Several Days and Put in Jail.

A Mob Gathers, But the Sheriff Removes Him to Franklin.

The Assumed Dispensers of Justice Go to That Place, But There They are Doomed to Defeat, as the Prisoner is Removed.
How a Sheriff Outdid Lynchers.
NASHVILLE, Tenn., June 18. — Amos Miller, a negro, about twenty-one years of age, was arrested at Santa Fe, Maury county, last Thursday, upon the charge of criminal assault on Mrs. Scott, a white woman. The deed is said to have been committed Friday, a week ago, but the officials were unable to catch Miller until Friday night, when he was placed in the jail at Columbia. Saturday night, the sheriff learning that a mob was on its way to the jail, slipped the negro out and took him to Franklin, Tenn. About 6 o'clock last evening, Sheriff Russell, of Williamson, got information that a mob composed of seventy-five or 100 men were en route to Franklin with the intention of mobbing Miller, so he and the jailer took the prisoner out and secreted him in a wheat field about half a mile from town, where they remained until 3 o'clock in the morning, when they returned to the jail with their prisoner. Early this morning the jailer took Miller to Mallory's station, and there boarded a train and brought him to Nashville. A mob visited the jail at 8 o'clock last night, but dispersed after finding their prisoner gone.
amos-miller-franklin-1888-06-19.A2:
TELEGRAMS TO THE STAR.
To Save a Prisoner from Lynching.
HARD WORK OF TENNESSEE OFFICERS IN TRYING TO
To Save a Prisoner from Lynching.
HARD WORK OF TENNESSEE OFFICERS IN INTRYING TO CIRCUMVENT A MOB.

NASHVILLE, TENN., June 21.—Amos Miller, colored, who was arrested at Santa Fe, Maury County, on the charge of having criminally assaulted Mrs. Scott, of that vicinity, was lodged in jail in this city yesterday to prevent his being lynched by a mob. Miller was first placed behind the bars in Columbia, but the sheriff learned that a mob was on the way to the jail and took the prisoner to Franklin. He received information that one hundred men were en route to Franklin with the intention of mobbing Miller, so he and the jailer took the prisoner out and secreted him in a wheat field about half a mile from town, where they remained until 8 o'clock in the morning, when they returned to the jail with their prisoner. Early yesterday morning the jailer took Miller to Mallory's Station and there boarded the train and brought him to Nashville. The mob entered Franklin about 8 o'clock Tuesday night and immediately went to the jail and demanded the prisoner. The turnkey opened the jail, and the mob visited every cell, but failing to find Miller, went out the Nashville turnpike to the first toll-gate, but learning there that the sheriff had not gone through, they returned to Franklin, and after waiting around the jail for two hours dispersed.

Took the Revolver for a Plaything.

CANONSBURG, PA., June 21.—A little boy named Williams, during the temporary absence of his parents, secured a revolver from a cloth pocket on the wall, and, being too young to know the dangerous nature of the weapon, placed it to his forehead and pulled the trigger. The ball took effect between the eyes. The child is in a critical condition.

He Dreamed of Garfield's Nomination.
AND NOW HE DREAMS THAT MCKINLEY WILL CARRY
OFF THE PRIZE AT CHICAGO.

PITTSBURG, June 21.—A special to the Post from Beaver Falls, Pa., says: This place can boast of the boss dreamer in the person of Jonathan Anderson, a well-known brewer. He has the wonderful facility of dreaming dreams that as a rule come true. Of late he has dreamed three times in succession that Major Wm. McKinley, of Ohio, had received the nomination at Chicago. Before the convention of 1880 Mr. Anderton dreamed that Garfield would be nominated. A few months ago he dreamed that his brewery was on fire. So realistic was the dream that he arose from bed and went to the brewery only to find it on fire.

Mike Johnson, confined in Dodge county jail under the charge of murder of another negro at the camps of the Amoskeag Lumber company several weeks since, and who was wounded himself by the man he killed, died in jail from the effects of his wound.

amos-miller-franklin-1888-06-19.A5:
THROUGH DIXIE.
The Week in the Sunny Southland.
The Death of an Old Miner—Angry Gamblers Get the Worst of a Row Started by Themselves.
GEORGIA.

"Uncle Dick," as he was commonly called, was an extraordinary man physically. He was near eighty years of age and never had a spell of sickness before. Has been on the mines around old Villa Rica for about fifty years, and the accident that befell him lately was the first that ever happened to him.

He leaves a wife and a large family of boys and girls to mourn his death, but fortunately he lived to see them all grown, his youngest a son now about eighteen years of age.

A party of negro gamblers, both sexes, who have been plying their trade at Glenmore, was reported to the authorities of Ware county by two respectable colored men named Grant and Parker. This incensed them to such a degree as that they armed themselves and swore vengeance against these men.

Monday night, with guns and pistols, they collected outside of a store in which Grant was setting, and sent one of their number in to assault him. The white men interfered in his behalf, and saved him from their clutches. Tuesday morning Constable McDonald attempted to arrest the ringleader of a mob that had collected, and menaced the peace of the town, when the negro reached for his hip pocket, whereupon the constable sent a bullet crashing through his shoulder, disabling him. Three more shots from the constable's trusty pistol succeeded in arresting the intended depredators of the mob, and eight of the leaders were arrested by Sheriff Henderson and a deputy, and safely lodged in Ware county jail at Waycross. All is now quiet at Glenmore.

News ereached here of the lynching of Ned Clark, colored, in Worth county. Clark was charged with attempting to commit a rape upon a young white girl thirteen years of age. His capturers were conveying him to Irwin county, the scene of his crime. They returned without him, stating that he had attempted to escape while in the woods and was shot down. His body was found with nineteen bullets in it, and the bushes around it were riddled with balls.

A special from Roswell Junction says: Our usual quiet community is somewhat aroused, by an attempt of rape, by a negro boy about 18 years old, known as Tom Cobb, who is working with Mr. Dave Fulcher, a farmer, living about two miles west of the place on the Roswell road.

Sunday night about 12 o'clock, Mr. Fulcher was awakenod by the screaming of one of his daughters sleeping in adjoining room with her sister, and a neighbor girl. She called her father telling him some one was in the room. He thought that they were only frightened probably from a dream, and told them to go to sleep, but they insisted and finally to pacify them, visited the room with a light, and under the bed, lay the negro Tom Cobb.
Mr. Fucher offered no act of violence but with determined coolness, arrested him, and sent for Mr. Marion Adams, a near neighbor, who assisted in guarding him until morning. They brought him to this place and was tried before Justice Elliott, and committed to Decatur jail in default of bond, to await his trial in August.

The negro offers no excuse for the act but claiming it to be somnambulism upon his part, nevertheless, he was wide awake when discovered under the bed.

Miss Fulcher says she was awakened by some one having hold of her hand. No attempt of lynching or violence has been spoken of whatever and doubtless the matter will rest quiet and allow the law to take the proper course.

A terrible railroad wreck occurred Thursday on the Savannah, Florida and Western railroad at the trestle over the Ochlocknee river, five miles from Thomasville. Freight train No. 25, consisting of four cars and the cab, had just crossed the river when about 400 feet of the trestle gave way, precipitating the entire train, except the engine, to the ground, twenty feet below. Fortunately, there were but four people on the train. The conductor and a negro brakeman were seriously injured. The negro will probably recover, but the conductor's injuries, though not necessarily fatal, are dangerous.

A special train from Thomasville was sent to the wreck as soon as possible, carrying a physician and all necessary help. The two injured men were carried to Thomasville and are doing well. The cause of the accident is not known, but the company is doing everything in its power for the men that were hurt. The cars are broken into splinters.

Amos Miller, the negro who raped Mrs. Scad in Maury county, has been caught and lodged in jail at Columbia. In an interview he admitted the deed, and told just how he accomplished it. He said that he had returned to see the daughter, who had in the meantime gone to the field with her father. He was disappointed in not finding her, but substituted the mother. There is great excitement, and it is not improbable that Miller will be lynched.

Ten years ago a man was found murdered, close to the railroad, a half mile from Kingston and near the residence of Mrs. J. Beck. He had been seen in the town several times, and had the appearance of being a well educated and refined gentleman. He was found murdered and stripped of his clothes. An inquest was held, and the jury agreed that the man met his death at the hands of some person unknown. No clew as to the identity of the man, nor any trace of the murderer, was ever found. An old negro man and woman testified that, coming up the railroad just after dark the night before the man was found murdered next day, they saw three men sitting around a camp fire, near the place of the murder. Several months—possibly a year—afterwards, a convict's suit of clothes was found hid away under some brush near by.

The circumstances suggest that one of the men camping was an escaped convict and murdered the man for his clothes in order to avoid detection by his stripes. The body of the murdered man was buried there and nothing more was ever heard of the circumstance until last week a lawyer from Greenville, S. C., was there tracing up the murder.

A fortune of 5,000 pounds was recently left by a relative in England to the only son of a widow lady living in Greenville, S. C. Her son left home ten years ago and has never since been heard from. She has engaged the services of this lawyer who has traced the young man to Atlanta, thence to Cartersville, then to Rome, back to Cartersville, then to Kingston and there he lost trace of him. The year and time of the murder corresponds with the time the young man left home. The widow lady is poor and of course if it can be proved that her son is dead she can come into possession of the legacy.

The first carload of watermelons passed through Atlanta on June 4th, about a week earlier than usual, and they are now going north, east and west at the rate of forty or fifty carloads a day.

The railroads are making preparations for immense shipments during the next twenty days, and "stray" cars are being called in for the transportation of this season's crop, which will surpass that of any previous year.

The question of time has been satisfactorily settled by the railroad managers, and the schedule for fruits and melons is a fast one, but the question of cars is one that requires constant attention from the agents of the various lines.

The raising of melons for shipment is proving very profitable, and the competition among the different transportation companies for the handling of this crop is growing more lively every day. This rivalry, of course, is friendly, and results only in benefit to the growers, insuring prompt delivery and all the facilities that can be commanded at this season of the year.
amos-miller-franklin-1888-06-19.A7:
Amos Miller, Who Outraged Mrs. Scott, of Maury County,
Hanged in a Court-Room in the Presence of the Judge.
His Brother Witnesses the Death of His Brutal Kinsman.
The Story of His Crime Retold Almost Justifies This Disregard for the Law-How the Villain Accomplished His Purpose.
FRANKLIN, Tenn., Aug. 10. — Amos Miller, the negro who outraged Mrs. Scott in Maury county lately, was lynched here about 10:30 o'clock this morning. It was thought best by the officers of the court not to attempt to try him at the regular session of the court and it was accordingly arranged to have a special session for his trial. Miller was brought here this morning from Nashville, where he has been held for safe keeping and arraigned in court. The mob had promised the officers of the court that if Miller was given a trial at once they would make no demonstrations, but let the law take its course. It seems, however, that

THE MOB WAS ORGANIZED

and held itself in readiness for action when the leaders gave the signal. Very soon after the court convened the leaders understood that the attorneys for the defense, Messrs. House and Henderson, were preparing to make a motion for a change of venue, and sent word to that affect to the mob. The court was proceeding to take up the case, and the attorney-general had announced himself as ready for the State, when the defendant's council applied for a continuance and proceeded to write an affidavit. At once an organized body of about fifty men, well armed, advanced to the court-house, entered the court-room, seized the negro and

SWUNG HIM TO A BANISTER RAIL
in the building almost in the very presence of the judge and the officers of the court. An effort was made to prevail upon the lynchers to desist but they were determined not to countenance anything that had the appearance of delay, and summarily executed their conception of justice. No one was allowed to interfere. A brother of Miller was in the courthouse and witnessed the hanging, but made no demonstration. Mrs. Scott was present at the trial but upon being notified left a few moments before the mob came.

None of the mob were disguised, and when they had executed their mission quietly dispersed. Intense excitement prevails throughout the town and county, but the result is nothing more than was expected by many of the people familiar with the details of the crime.

THE CRIME
for which Miller was lynched was committed on the 10th of June. Mrs. Scott, the victim of the criminal assault, is a resident of Maury county. Miller, who was twenty-one years old, and had been employed on a farm near Hillsboro, visited the residence of Mrs. Scott and asked for something to eat, securing some bread and milk. Miller then proceeded some distance from the house and concealed himself in the bushes until he observed Mr. Scott, the husband of the woman, leaving his home. Returning to Mrs. Scott's Miller attacked her and accomplished his design. She stated that she first attempted to drive Miller away, but he refused to go; then she attempted to escape, whereupon he seized her until she became unconscious. Miller fled immediately after committing the crime, and although diligent search for him was made by Mr. Scott and many neighbors the negro evaded arrest for a week. He was then taken to jail in Columbia, where he admitted his guilt. It was subsequently learned that his intention was to outrage the person of Mrs. Scott's daughter, but finding she had left in company with her father, Miller then determined to force the mother to submit to him. Several attempts have been made since Miller's arrest to lynch him, but they proved futile until today.

LYNCHED A NEGRO. A Girl Accuses him of Assault and a Mob Takes him in Hand.
ASHEVILLE, July 15.—Yesterday about 1 o'clock a rumor reached here that an assault had been committed on Sallie Kate Parker, a white girl, 13 years of age, by a negro, in the northern suburbs of the city. The police were notified, and the country and town were searched closely for the guilty man. About 9 o'clock last night a negro named John Humphreys was arrested under strong suspicion. The girl had said that the negro had on a striped shirt and was barefooted. When arrested Humphreys had on a white shirt and shoes, but it was ascertained that he had taken off a striped shirt and put on a white one, and had put on shoes.

He was made to put on a striped shirt and take off the shoes, and was taken at once into the presence of the girl, who identified him immediately. The negro was then locked up in the city calaboose. Considerable excitement prevailed at the time, and whispers of lynching were heard. In order to avoid this, at 1 o'clock this morning the negro was put in the steel cage of the county jail.

About 3:15 A. M. a band of from twenty-five to forty masked men came to the jail, and before Deputy Sheriff James Worley, who had the jail in charge, was aware of it they were in the jail. He grabbed a gun and ran to the top of the steps and opened fire on the crowd, which was returned with a shower of bullets. The walls of the jail show that there was considerable firing, but no one was hurt as far as ascertained. Worley was overpowered, but would not give the combination to the cage lock.

The mob, being prepared with sledge hammers and crowbars, literally tore the cage to pieces, occupying fully an hour in doing it. They then took the negro out and hanged him to a tree about a quarter of a mile from the jail, within the city limits. As soon as released Sheriff Worley rang the fire bell, and soon headed a posse and tried to recover the prisoner, but was eluded by the mob.

The girl was waylaid on her way from town in a hollow in the woods. The negro crept up behind her and choked her. The girl's throat and face were torn. It is rumored that the negro made a full confession of his guilt before he was hanged.

asheville-asheville-1888-09.A8:
A New Company that Fills a long Felt Want.
From the Raleigh Observer.

In these days when experience and a sense of proper caution has made the rule and custom of requiring "bonds" from their employees almost imperative among business corporations and individuals, the absence of an "Indemnity Company," such as is well known in other localities, has been severely felt in this State. Many men who could otherwise readily command position of trust cannot obtain them for the reason that they shrink from asking their relations and friends from going on their bonds, &c, whereas owing to the facilities offered by an "Indemnity Company" they are relieved from any embarrassment of that kind, since by paying the small premium required by the company an "indemnifying bond" issued in favor of the employer, absolutely guarantees the latter from any possibility of loss. It is with much pleasure, therefore, that we welcome into our midst that popular and well known indemnity company, "The Fidelity and Casualty Company," of New York, which has just entered North Carolina with Mesers F. H. Cameron & Co., of this city, as general managers for the State, to whom all correspondence should be addressed. The fact that over thirty-five thousand of the leading banks, railroads, manufacturers, merchants and other business men of this country are patrons of the company speak for itself.

Potts' effort to Escape the Gallows.—WASHINGTON, N. C., July 13.—W. A. Potts, Jr., a young lawyer, who was to have been hanged here 10-day, attempted suicide last night by taking morphine. He was found by one of the prisoners about 6 o'clock this morning in an unconscious condition. The Sheriff was notified and medical aid promptly called in. On examination the doctors pronounced him in a dying condition. In a short time, however, he rallied and showed signs of recovery, and by 10 a.m. there was no doubt of his full and complete recovery. The Sheriff, recognizing his feeble condition, wired Gov. Scales for a respite until next week, to which an almost immediate reply was received granting the respite until the 17th. Potts had written a letter to the Sheriff thanking him for his kindness and stating that he had relieved him (the Sheriff) of a painful duty, also stating that the physicians were in no wise responsible for possession of the drug. Upon the reception of the respite from Gov. Scales the Sheriff placed a death-watch over the prisoner, with rigid instructions to allow him to see no one except the physicians. He made no response upon being told of his respite except to ask for how long it was granted. Potts states that he took between 25 and 30 grains of morphine, but the attending physicians say he could not have taken over 2 to 3.

[Potts again got hold of poison on Tuesday, took it, and died soon afterwards, cheating the gallows at last. Poor fellow.]

The Democrats of Craven county have nominated for the Senate Mr H. S. Nunn, editor of the Newbern Journal, and for the House, Messrs J. W. Lane, Joel Kinsey and R. A. Russell.

[If the people of Craven would elect Mr Nunn and his colleagues, they would do themselves credit and greatly benefit their county.]

The choice of J. H. Dobson, Esq., of Surry, as elector in the Fifth district, is first rate in all respects.

The Democrats of the 36th Senatorial district, composed of the counties of Burke, Caldwell, McDowell, Mitchell and Yancey, are promptly in the field with their candidates, Messrs Hartwell S. Blair of Caldwell, and S. B. Briggs of Yancey, having been nominated. The nominees are most worthy gentlemen and were paid the compliment of a rising vote. Mr J. G. Bynum of Morganton, was chairman of the convention, and Mr D. Elliott of Bakersville, secretary. Prof. W. E. Abernethy of Burke, nominated Mr Blair and W. H. Bower in behalf of Caldwell county seconded the nomination, and presented the name of Mr Briggs.

Another Abjuration of Radicalism. — KINSTON, N. C., July 14.—At a meeting of the Cleveland and Fowle Club here last night F. B. Loftin, Esq., ex-Republican representative from this Senatorial district, was duly enrolled as a member, and in an eloquent speech stated that he would ever hereafter give his allegiance to the Democratic party. This action means a Democratic gain of several Republican votes. Truly the "G. O. P." is in a state of rapid disintegration.

In concluding a short sketch on the political outlook in the north-western part of the State, and noticing the condition in Watauga, Ashe, Alleghany, Alexander and Wilkes, the Statesville Landmark gives this good news: "In all the counties named the nomination of Judge Fowle is the most acceptable one that could have been made, and if the balance of the State will do its duty as they will do theirs he will have the largest majority that has been secured in the State since the war."

The Chicago Times thinks the old red bandana will see many years of usefulness. It thus speaks of his age: "The great age of Mr Thurman, who is but seventy-four or seventy-five, is set down as a serious objection to his candidacy. He has outlived the allotted time, it is true, but longevity is not so extraordinary as to warrant the idea that an old age of usefulness is not a possibility. John Adams, who was President of the United States, died at ninety-one years of age. Thomas Jefferson lived to be eighty-three. James Madison died at eighty-five. John Quincy Adams was eighty when he fell at his post of duty in the House of Representatives, for, after serving as President, he did not think it beneath his dignity (as surely it was not) to serve a constituency in Congress. Jackson was seventy-eight when he died. Martin Van Buren was eighty.

Two years ago the prohibitionists of Guilford county headed by Dr. Benbow, chairman of the Prohibition Executive Committee, and assisted by Walker, the candidate for Governor, ran, as we are informed, a prohibition ticket in that county. What was the result? Simply the defeat of the Democratic ticket, and the election of the Radical ticket in Guilford county. Benbow is trying the same game this year for the State at large. He has always been a Radical, and he knows that the only way to defeat the Democratic party and to elect the Radical ticket is to divide the Democratic party on the Prohibition issue.—Concord Times.

The Democrats of Craven, joined by many from the adjoining counties, assembled in Newbern to ratify and endorse the nomination of the State and National conventions. Fowle, Finger, Sanderlin, Davidson, James A. Bryan and C. C. Clark spoke.

In pursuance of a suggestion made by the North Carolina delegation, at the meeting of the National Association of Democratic clubs at Baltimore, it has been decided by a Central Committee, to at once begin correspondence with the various clubs in the State with a view to calling a convention of the State clubs to be held about August 15th at some accessible point. It should be understood, however, that a convention will not be called unless a sufficient number of clubs favor it.

CONCORD, July 16.—The court house was filled to-night to hear Mr W. T. Walker, prohibition candidate for Governor, and Hon. W. M. Robbins who, by courtesy speaks on the occasion. Mr Walker ably presented his cause, political, third party, and prohibition. Maj. Robbins ably presented his cause. Local option, prohibition and Democratic supremacy in North Carolina. The audience was good and the speakers were conciliatory.

LATEST NEWS ITEMS.
Wm. Houston (col.) will be hung at Winston July 19th. The commissioners have ordered a public execution.

The Maxton Union says that for the first time in its history Robeson county was without a licensed bar-room on the 4th of July.

A census of Salisbury has been taken. It shows that the town has 4,159 inhabitants, an increase since 1885—three years—of 755.

The State Convention of the Farmer's Alliance will be held in Raleigh August 14th. It will be a great gathering of North Carolina's best men and Raleigh will be glad to welcome them.

Three children of Mr. P. C. Hall, of Hickory, were out driving last week. The horse became frightened, began to run and kick—the children fell out of the buggy and were badly hurt, wounded and bruised.

The Progressive Farmer denies the report that the negroes are joining the Farmer's Alliance. The Alliance allows only white men to join. The negroes have organized an Alliance of their own, but it has no connection with the white Alliance.

A negro named Humphreys attempted to rape a white girl near Asheville last Saturday. He was arrested and lodged in jail. At night a party of lynchers broke open the jail and lynched the negro near the town of Asheville. It was swift retribution for the most heilish of hellish crimes.

James Byers, convicted of murder, was hung at Wilkesboro, Wilkes county, July 13th. Thousands of people witnessed the execution. Never before was such a scene witnessed in Wilkesboro. Men, women and children flocked to see the execution. Byers was much depressed. He died in six minutes after the trap fell.

The Raleigh District Conference (M. E Church) was held at Selma last week. The CHRONICLE's information is that it was a very pleasant and profitable occasion and that the hospitality of the people of Selma was unbounded. Bishop Dunean presided and State Treasurer Donald W. Bain was Secretary. On Sunday Bishop Dunean preached to a large congregation and raised $800 to pay the debt on the Selma Methodist church.

At Goldsboro last Friday night a man by the name of Bud Anderson struck Mr. W. H. Porter on the head with a ponderous rock, crushing his skull and knocking him senseless to the ground. Mr. Porter was carried home where he died at 7 o'clock Saturday morning. The occasion of the killing was this: Porter kept a lunch stand and declined to sell to Anderson on a credit. About an hour afterwards Anderson crept up behind Porter and killed him. Anderson is in jail. Great sympathy is felt for the family of Mr. Porter, who was a quiet and honest citizen.

Essex County is small in population and wealth, but will be influential in the present legislature, through the calibre of her representatives. Senator Mansur will hold a prominent position in the Senate as member of the Judiciary Committee, and Chairman of the Committee on Military Affairs. The Committee appointments of the House are not yet made public, but we expect Speaker Grout will not fail to recognize the claims of our county.

Never has the Legislature assembled under better promise of valuable work to be done than the one now in session. The large number of able and prominent men who are members of either branch is an assurance that much will be accomplished; that helps and restraints will in various lines of statutory law be given where able, legal men of experience see there is most need. The re-election of Speaker Grout, clerk Stickney and secretary Brownell is a surety that the business will be done with promptness and accuracy.

The report of Inspector of Finance, Page, presents some interesting facts in figures: Deposits in Savings Banks and Trust Companies, June 30, 1888, $16,602,067; June 30, 1886, $14,253,963; Resident depositors hold of the first mentioned sum $13,888,186; non-residents $2,713,881. The, we believe, growing evil of investing these deposits in western mortgages is best shown by figures taken from a table in the report. Amount thus invested:

1879.....$1,278,399 1881.....$2,219,696
1883.....3,950,143 1885.....4,774,872
1887.....6,225,903 1888.....6,563,797

A five-fold increase in ten years, while the increase of deposits has been only two-fold!

House Bill No. 3 comes from the able Commission appointed by the Governor under an Act of 1886, and from a cursory examination it meets our approval. Briefly stated, it provides for a State Superintendent as now, a county superintendent who has immediate supervision of the schools in his county; an equalization of taxation; that no applicant less than 18 years of age shall receive a certificate; the State tax is raised to 18 cents on a dollar, and the district system and organization is retained. These are some of the main features and are all good ones, but discussion will bring opposition, and we shall have occasion to refer to this matter again. In the meantime our columns are open for the discussion.

The messages of Gov. Ormsbee and Gov. Dillingham before the Legislature, and by the press given to the people, in a lucid and tangible style present the leading topics which for the next few weeks will claim the attention of our law makers, in fact all of our citizens.

One of the topics to which they both give attention is one in which there is a wide interest, and which is of the most vital importance to the State. The matter of education, how to better our schools, get more of the worth of our money, and give to our boys and girls the best possible advantages, are questions worthy of consideration. All, or nearly all the leading educators of the State are thoroughly ashamed of the lack of progressive action, yes, even the decline which is apparent to all who value education more than money, who are ambitious for a higher and broader education for the to be men and women of the future, than was in past time accorded to those who now are the fathers and mothers. We are glad for the exertions and discussions of the past. The question is open and still invites the best thought of the best men and women.

The difference between the Republican and Democratic propositions to revise the tariff is this: The Republicans propose to revise it to

meet the natural changes in business life without affecting the principle of protection to American industries which they believe in; the Democrats propose to revise it so as to make it "a tariff for revenue only," claiming that "protection does not protect," and that "our industries need no protection." The President's letter of acceptance again supplies the proof of this when it says "the absolute duty of limiting the rate of tariff charges to the necessities of a frugal and economical administration of the government seems to be perfectly plain." The issue, therefore, is "protection or free trade."

Cheap goods are desirable, but to have them labor must be made cheaper. And to cut wages means to reduce the buying power of the masses, and a change on their part to a less comfortable and more pinching style of living. Is a wholesale move of this sort what the working people of the nation are ready to vote for?

THE "LAND OF THE SKY."

Between the outlying buttresses of the Blue Ridge and the persistent chain of the Smoky Mountains, lies the true Western North Carolina. Here the Blue Ridge by one grand upheaval reaches its limit. Its summit is the "Land of the Sky," looking down in sublime composure on the wilderness of mountains at its feet, clothed to their very tops with forests. In these woods we have seen the poplar tree 8 feet in diameter; then there are walnut, cherry and beech, some oak, hickory and birch, and occasionally we might think ourselves in Vermont, for we meet with the hemlock, the majestic pine, and that tree always associated with happy days, the sugar maple, and they have actually made maple sugar here. This is surely a grand store house, and it only remains for the railroad to cut a passage to it. How much a few weeks of snow would be worth here! We have found some curious stones, and are informed that the mountains hold garnet, quartz, emerald, beryl, topaz, amethyst and other rare stones; and gold, iron and nickel are already being mined. These mountains are covered with a deep rich soil making, when clear, profitable farming lands. Sheep raising seems a promising industry in these broad ranges, sheltered from severe storms, and abounding in mountain streams.
using industry in these broad ranges, sheltered from severe storms, and abounding in mountain streams. Poultry raising is quite important, and they raise all the fruits usually found in intermediate climates. The people exist on what they raise almost entirely. One man said he did not see $10 in cash the year round. There is about an equal proportion of whites and negroes, and they are quite distinct in everything. At Asheville, the chief part of this section, the saloons are plainly designated "The White Man's Bar," or "The Black Man's Bar." This recalls an incident that occurred in a white man's bar during our stay in the city. A German had in connection with his saloon some native animals, among them two young bears. One Sunday before going to dinner he neglected to put young bruins back in their cage. Finding themselves master of the situation they concluded to go on a free drunk. Accordingly they knocked over a case of French brandy and lapped up the beverage. It took them about the same period that it takes a man to reach a state of intoxication under the same conditions, and then they proceeded exactly on his plan. They knocked each other over, threw bottles across the room, smashed the glasses and mirror, and caused damage to the amount of about $200. "Verily, it is good alike for man and beast." We happened in Asheville during a desperate season. The night previous to our arrival the jail was raided and a negro hung very informally to a poplar tree. It was for an act which should justify lynch law everywhere, for it is an improvement on some court decisions we know of, but we can't help the question, "Would they do so by a white man?"

In my next I will briefly describe Asheville, also a trip to some places in this "Land of the Sky."

KARL HENRY.

horrible Fate.
ATHENS GA. Feb. 3.—The inhabitants of
ATHENS, GA., Feb. 3.—The inhabitants of East Athens were horror-stricken to-day when it became known that a negro had attempted to outrage the beautiful little daughter of Mr. O'Kelly. Miss O'Kelly, a most lovely young lady, was returning to her home, about three miles from here, when she met a large negro man who commenced talking to her, using very obscene and offensive language. At last he attacked her to satisfy his brutal desire but she broke from his embrace and ran toward her home, screaming at the top of her voice. The negro seeing that if he pursued he would be caught, fled in the opposite direction. The young lady arrived at her home thoroughly exhausted. She succeeded, however, in making known to her father what had happened, and in a few moments a posse of men started in search of the negro. He is supposed to be hidden near George Murrel's plantation, on the Georgia railroad. The people in that section are thoroughly aroused over this bold attempt and declare with one accord that when the negro is caught the verdict of Judge Lynch shall be carried out. Mr. O'Kelly is a Justice of the Peace, and is a most worthy gentleman and faithful officer. Up to 9 o'clock to-night the hunt is still going on, but the negro has not been caught.

GEORGIA AND FLORIDA.
NEWS OF THE TWO STATES TOLD
IN PARAGRAPHS.
Gordon county's delegates favor the re-election of Congressman Clements.
The Macon china store has sold out to James Carhart and J. W. Domingos.
Sixteen persons joined the First Presbyterian church at Macon on last Sunday.
The contract for the new opera house at Thomasville was closed Monday with Mr. Gunn, a theatrical contractor.
At the convention held in Banks county Tuesday, Hon. J. N. Coggins was nominated to represent the county in the next legislature.
There came very near being serious trouble at Lithonia Saturday night between the whites and blacks who work at Venable's mountain.
At the mass meetings of the Douglas and Newton county democracy Tuesday Hon. John D. Stewart was indorsed for re-election to congress.
Col. Frank P. Rice and Judge W. R. Hammond have entered on a lively competition for the senatorial nomination in the Atlanta district.
E. L. Michael of Athens has a pigeon that is trained to do almost anything he tells it. It can play on the piano, waltz, march and crow like a rooster.
The Third Georgia regiment reunion, at Madison, on Aug. 8 and 9, is an assured success, $800 having already been subscribed, beside quite a number of carcasses for the barbecue.
It is said that the firm of Masterson & Chapman of Macon has dissolved, W. B. Chapman buying the interest of Wallace Masterson, and will continue the business at the same place.
While Moses Morris and S. Hayes were driving on Prince avenue, at Athens, on Sunday, the king bolt of the buggy broke. Mr. Hayes was pitched from the vehicle and was badly bruised.
A few mornings ago L. W. Dixon of La Crosse entered his store and discovered that there was a snake stretched out on the counter quietly waiting for customers to come in for it to serve them.
William Chambless says that there are four or five alligators in the swamp on his place, four or five miles from Americus, and that they are ripe enough to kill, as they are going for his pigs.
Capt. J. E. Markett of Sumter county, who has been confined to his room for a month or more, was in American Monday, greatly improved, but he was still paralyzed in his left leg and right arm, though still hopeful of ultimate recovery.

Among the passengers on the Northeastern road Monday were a German accompanied by his wife and seven children. They had come direct from the fatherland; could sneak no English, and at Athens their destination could not be learned.

A. G. Elder and Jack Jackson of Occone county had a little fistiuff on Jackson street, Athens, Monday. The Marquis of Queensbury rules were not observed. Jackson got a blow on his head that brought the blood. The fight was about a debt.

The counties in the Ninth congressional district elected delegates to the congressional convention Tuesday. The following were instructed for Hon. Allen D. Candler: Cherokee, White and Gilmur. Habersham went for Hon. George N. Lester by four majority. Gwinett's delegates are for Peeples first and Candler second.

A few mornings ago Mrs. Ransome Holloway, whose husband is cropping with G. H. Walker near LaCrosse, returns from milking the cows to discover that a snake about four feet long, known as a rattlesnake's pilot, equal in every description to the genuine rattler, except it has no rattles, was quietly resting in the bed with two of her children. The children were removed and the snake killed without any serious damage.

A fire broke out in the engine house of the wagon factory of Blount & Hill at East Point, near Atlanta, Tuesday. The engine house, which is a brick structure, was destroyed before the flames could be subdued. The heat was so intense that there was some fear that the boiler might burst. The damage, it was thought, will amount to $1,000. The main building was not damaged. The origin of the fire is unknown, but the building is supposed to have caught from the fire in the furnace.

The executive committee of the democratic party of Thomas county met Tuesday and fixed the time for the primary election, which is to nominate two candidates for the legislature, and to transact other business. The primary has been called for July 28. A mass meeting of the party is called for Aug. 4, to elect delegates to the gubernatorial, congressional and senatorial conventions; to elect an executive committee for the two years next ensuing, and to transact such other business as may come before the meeting.
Miss Mary Johnson, a school teacher of Atlanta, was tried in a justice's court Tuesday, under an indictment for assault and battery, in that she had whipped a small boy, named Emmett Atkinson, who was a pupil in her school. Miss Johnson was a teacher in the fourth grade in the Marietta street school. The whipping took place on April 10, last, and the next day the father of the lad who was chastised took out a warrant for Miss Johnson, charging her with assault and battery. The defendant was bound over, and Tuesday she appeared in court to answer to the charge. She was acquitted.

Sunday night a horse which was hitched in Tockwotten, near Thomasville, was mounted by an unknown negro, and ridden off in the direction of Tallahassee. Monday morning the horse was found lying dead in the road near the five-mile post, with the saddle and bridle on. It is quite evident that the horse had been ridden perhaps all night, and that the negro was returning, as the horse's head was toward town. A negro was seen hanging around in the woods near where the horse was for several hours. He asked two or three parties if the horse was dead, but was not seen to go near the animal. He was evidently the negro who perpetrated the outrage.

The following letter was received by the deputy United States marshal at Albany:

"MILLER COUNTY, Ga., July 2, 1888. I write to you for protection. My husband is murdered, and murdered by the kuklux. They have threatened my son's life and he is about fifteen years old. I can prove who they are. Please come at once. I live in Miller county, southwest of Minis' mill, in Baker county. I look to you for protection for my house.

(Signed) ELIZABETH BARFIELD."

When the news of Barfield's murder was received here it was stated that he was killed by a deputy sheriff while resisting arrest. About the same time a band of Miller county regulators posted a plantation in Baker, warning all hands to leave under penalty of death. The laborers were all armed with rifles by the proprietors and remained.

Tuesday about 8 o'clock a.m., near Tyty, a station about eighty miles from Waycross, on the Brunswick and Western railroad, a colored man named Ben Walker was found in the road dead. He was employed as a hand at a saw mill in that vicinity. He had been shot in the face and neck with buckshot. He was not cold when found. It is thought that he was shot after daylight. He was a very quarrelsome negro, and had only a few days ago had a difficulty with some white men. The coroner's jury held an inquest over his body, but failed to develop any clue to the perpetrators. The general feeling is that he has met his just deserts, and that others may profit by the example.

Democrats of Clarke county have hard work ahead of them to prevent the election of W. A. Pledger, colored, to the legislature. He has announced himself as a candidate, and the negroes are rallying to his support. There is danger of his election, as the defaulting tax list shows more white than colored voters. The democrats are alarmed about the outlook, while the republicans are enthusiastic. Pledger is a sharp negro, and will poll the entire colored vote.

The Richmond county mass meeting to select delegates to the gubernatorial and senatorial convention was the stormiest political meeting held in the county in many years. The usual custom has been to hold mass meetings at twelve o'clock in the day. But, by some chance, this one was called for night. The Knights of Labor from the factory district took advantage of the change, and were down in numbers to capture the meeting. When the hour arrived for the meeting the factory element predominated in the crowd, and they were ready with their little slate. Just as soon as the programme opened, Mr. E. J. O'Conner was nominated for chairman. They immediately nominated Mr. Silas C. Reed, and overwhelmingly elected him.

Judge Claiborne Snead offered resolutions pledging Richmond county to the rotation
J. H. Nehbeng made a speech, declaring that the registration law had disfranchised the poor people of the county, and they proposed to send delegates to the legislature and senate who would rightly represent them; that Martin V. Calvin and John Davidson were to blame for the iniquitous law.

Captain W. B. Young, of the unterrified democracy, said he believed in doing justice to everybody.

Davis, of the Knights of Labor, interrupting: "If they had justice they'd be in the penitentiary." [Yells of applause.]

Mr. Young continued his defense of Senator Davidson, declaring that the bill was before the legislature for two terms. Never once was there a word or letter of objection from any constituent.

Hon. J. R. Lamar gained the floor, and said he was there to take the full responsibility for the bill, and any condemnation that such responsibility entailed.

The knights yelled for the previous question. It is impossible to describe the scene that followed. The chairman and Mr. Lamar sprang upon the table, and for half an hour there was nothing but yells and shoutings, Lamar claiming to have the floor, and refusing to yield it, and the knights going ahead and passing their resolution and electing a ticket and adjournment amid yells. They bore Chairman Silas Reed on their shoulders from the hall, and up Broad street, shouting and yelling and stopping at the street corners, and having short harrangues from their leaders.

Mr. Lamar held the floor to the last, and when they withdrew Mr. C. H. Cohen nominated Mr. E. J. O'Conner as chairman, and the following delegates were elected to the senatorial convention: J. L. Maxwell, L. T. Blome, S. P. Weisger, W. H. Foster, C. S. Bohler, Egene O'Conner; also, a resolution asking a modification of the rotation system. Governor Gordon's administration was indorsed, and the following delegates elected to the gubernatorial convention: W. I. Dolph, Z. W. Carwile, C. Henry Cohen, M. V. Calvin, Robert L. Pierce, Frank W. Capers, James M. Tago, William F. Eve, P. J. O'Conner, D. Sancker, W. H. T. Walker, C. A. Robie and R. J. Wilson. The meeting adjourned, and is the subject of conversation all over town. No such meeting has ever been held in Augusta before.

A difficulty took place at Hartsfield's mill, in Colquitt county, about twelve miles from Camilla Wednesday. A large concourse from Colquitt, Camilla and East Mitchell county gathered to celebrate the fourth with a picnic and barbecue. The Camilla brass band furnished the music. Everything passed pleasantly until the barbecue was served at 2 o'clock. An altercation occurred between two Mitchell and Colquitt county boys. The lie was passed and resented. Friends interfered, when one man was hit and knocked down. Instantly all was a scene of confusion. Pistols, knives, clubs, boards and every kind of weapon was pressed into service. About thirty shots were exchanged. The scene was heart-rending. Women and children were weeping for fear their loved ones would be killed; others were flying in every direction.

A. H. Jones, a prominent stock raiser of Mitchell county, was shot in the left breast three inches below the collar bone by Allison Cellier. The wound will likely prove fatal. Cellier was shot through the right ear and badly beaten over the head. Jim Jones, of Colquitt county, was shot in the back between the shoulder blades and had his upper lip badly disfigured by a piece of scanling. His wounds are considered dangerous. A. J. Moree was reported badly cut in several places. A lady, in attempting to escape, was shot through the hair. During the confusion the band stand broke down and the instruments ruined. The band struck a bee line for home.
Many of the old soldiers, those who did some of the fighting, met at Blakely Thursday, and amid the din of drums and boom of cannon, unfurled the stars and stripes from our ninety-foot confederate flag pole, now standing in the United States. Union soldiers stationed here in 1865 started to cut it down, but were warned not to do it and desisted.

THE WHEN THE TEXAS METHOD. A Wealthy Texan Stabs Three Elkhart Citizens, One of Whom Will Probably Die.
ELKHART, Aug. 3.—Benjamin Scott, a wealthy Texan who came here a few weeks ago to look after property which he owns, unprovokedly stabbed three men here this afternoon at 4:30, and is now in jail at Goshen, the county-seat. He owns property in the rear of the Clifton House, and had been quarreling with several persons on the ground that they were trespassing, stating on various occasions that he would do some stabbing. Con Crowley, a young stock-dealer, who occupied a bara near Scott's property, and Geo. Newell, a leading farmer and capitalist, who owns property adjoining, were in an alley, discussing the alleged trespass in an apparently friendly manner, when Scott said he would stab the first man who again infringed on his land. Crowley replied that only a cur would use a knife, when Scott immediately pulled out a large pocket knife and plunged it three times into Crowley's abdomen. Newell immediately seized a club and rushed to Crowley's assistance, when Scott sprang at him, before he could use the club, and thrust the knife into his left lung and gave him a wicked slash across the back. James Smith, colored porter at the Clifton House, terrified by the transaction, endeavored to rush by Scott and escape, though only a spectator, but the infuriated man caught him and struck him in the side, inflicting a bad but not dangerous cut. Scott then started up street on a run, until James Bemis told him to surrender, which he declined to do, with the remark that he would also kill Bemis, as he came from a country where they did such things. Bemis, however, knocked him down with a powerful blow and took the knife from him. Crowley walked out of the alley and started up Main street, but he had not proceeded far when he fell into the gutter, from which he arose and stood up, when he fell again, unconscious, and was taken home in that condition. He is still unconscious, and his death is now momentarily expected. Newell was taken to a physician, where his wounds were attended to, after which he was removed to his home. He is dangerously hurt, but his exact condition is not yet known. Scott is about forty-five years of age and not a vicious looking man, though he has threatened, the past few weeks, to stab several persons, and he boasts that he came from Texas, where they kill. The streets are full of people to-night, and the expression is that the officers did not take Scott to Goshen any too soon.

Matthew Byrnes Had Trouble with His Girl, and Said He Would Do the Brodie Act—His Leap, 160 Feet, Beats All—Bruised but Otherwise All O. K.

A strongly built, good looking young man was seen to run along the north roadway of the Brooklyn Bridge about 10:25 yesterday morning, jump nimbly over the outer guard rail and walk up the big cable that stretches away toward the western tower. He climbed up until he was fifteen feet above the roadway. He had thrown off his hat and coat before going over the guard rail, and had thereby attracted the attention of Bridge Policeman Brett, who was on patrol on the promenade at the middle span. The spot where the young man had first appeared is the highest part of the bridge. Brett, realizing that another bridge jumper was before him, shouted to the man to get down and waved his club at him frantically. The man waved back his hands in mock adieu, and then, looking up the river, he jumped out. His legs were close together, and his hands were held straight up over his head. He shot down like an arrow until within about fifteen feet of the water, when he turned a summersault and thumped into the water on his left arm near the shoulder. The spray flew up fifteen or twenty feet. When he reappeared he struck out as though intending to swim to shore, but his strokes were weak, and, after a few attempts, he turned over on his back and floated along with the tide.

Policeman Brett in the mean time had climbed over from the promenade to the roadway, and had questioned the drivers of two trucks who had seen the man jump. It was from one of these trucks that the jumper had made his break for the cable. One was going to New York and one to Brooklyn. The drivers were pale and frightened, and Brett was too hurried to ask many questions. He picked up the jumper's discarded hat, leaving the coat lying on the roadway, and jumping on the truck going to New York, ordered the driver to whip up. This truck belongs to Howell & Saxton, the iron railing firm. Mr. Howell is the President of the bridge trustees, and it was probably his truck that the young man rode over on. Brett informed Roundsman Wiggins, and the two ran to the Dover street pier to see what had become of the jumper. They saw him picked up by the tug Cheney, which was towing the excursion barges of St. John's Guild, and later saw him transferred near Governor's Island to the tug John Berwind.

The man was supposed by the Captain of the tug to be in a critical condition. He was taken to Hamilton ferry in Brooklyn, and thence in an ambulance to the Long Island College Hospital. Dr. Shaw, the superintendent, questioned him and learned that the jumper was Matthew Byrnes, aged 21. His weight was placed on the blotter as 160 pounds, his height at 5 feet 7 inches, and his nativity, Ireland. He wore a brown shirt of Jersey cloth which had striking purple stripes, and brown trousers, with black silk stripes on the outer long seams. A physical examination showed only two trifling bruises, one on the right shoulder and one on the left shoulder. He was suffering somewhat from the shock, but had no internal injuries.

"What did you jump for?" he was asked.

"Oh, for fun," was the reply. "I used to jump from the cliffs in Ireland, and I knew I could do it without hurting myself. Besides, I am a strong swimmer."

He said that he had not attempted suicide, but had hoped to gain some work through the notoriety the feat would bring him.

"I suppose I'll get sent to Crow Hill for this," he said. "but I'm satisfied to live on the county's bounty for a month." He said that he had worked in a stable at Port Richmond, but recently he had been living elsewhere with some friends. A search of his clothes revealed nothing but a tintype picture of himself. A number of injections of morphine quieted him, and he will probably be arraigned in court to-day.

Somewhat over a year ago Matt Byrnes, as he is known among his acquaintances, applied for work at the livery stable of M. E. Wygant at 6 Jewett avenue, Port Richmond. He was a strong, pleasant-featured lad, and Mr. Wygant engaged him as a stable hand. He had not been there long before he made the acquaintance of Katie Smith, a pretty 19-year-old girl, who lives with her widowed mother and two sisters at 3 Bennett avenue, Port Richmond. Katie has dark hair, black eyes and eyelashes, pretty features, and a slender form. She accepted Byrnes's advances in a modest way, neither encouraging nor repelling him. She seemed to like him, and, after much pressing on his part, she consented to marry him. In the mean time she continued to assist her mother and sisters to earn their livelihood by diligent sewing. Through his connection with the livery stable Byrnes was often able to take Miss Smith driving. Last May, while they were driving through St. George, he pointed out the Brooklyn Bridge to Katie, and said he wouldn't be surprised if he jumped from it some day. Miss Smith laughed.

Her attachment for him grew less as she noticed that he was eccentric in his speech. One day she said to him:

"Matt. I am surprised at the way you fib. You have told me some awful stories."

"I know it, Katie," he replied. "Every man has got his failings, and lying is mine."

Finally she told him she could not marry him. He pleaded with her, but she would not relent. He had been discharged by Wygant for indulging in too much "moonshine," as the latter expressed it yesterday, and for allowing the horses to run away with him several times. He then secured work from James Brown, a West Brighton liveryman, and after that from James Bailey, a farmer. He did not keep this place long either, as Mr. Bailey objected to his long and deep meditations when he should have been at work. One day Joseph Bailey, the farmer's son, said to him:

"Matt, you've got to decide between bumming and working."

Land" Criminals.

TOPEKA, KAN., Aug. 7.—The six men arrested for complicity in the killing of Sheriff Cross in "No Man's Land," were arrested on a warrant charging them with conspiring on Kansas soil to take the life and property of other citizens. The court has no jurisdiction over the territory of "No Man's Land," hence the murderers cannot be arrested for murder, but it is thought the fact of conspiracy can be established against them under the United States law. The penalty for this offense is imprisonment if the penitentiary for a term not exceeding ten years. The men are J. P. Chamberlin, chairman of the Stevens County Commissioners; Sam, Robinson, city marshal of Hugoton; G. W. Donald, L. E. Cook, J. E. Cook, and one other whose name is not given. The prisoners will probably reach Topeka today and will have an examination before the United States Commissioner.

THE PERILS OF GAS.

An Entire Residence Destroyed by an Explosion.

Explosion.

GALENA, ILL., Aug. 7.—A terrific explosion of gas occurred yesterday afternoon in the cellar of the double brick residence on Prospect street in this city, occupied by the families of D. W. Atchison, pastor of the First Methodist Episcopal Church, and Charles E. Haile, a merchant. The entire structure, which was quickly set on fire, was partially destroyed and much of the contents burned, including the valuable library of Mr. Atchison. The latter's son, 7 years old, was badly, though not fatally, injured by flying debris. The loss will probably reach $6,000, and is nearly covered by insurance.

Ike Weir's Coming Fight.

NEW YORK, Aug. 7.—A light for $1,000 a side was arranged yesterday between like Weir, the "Belfast Spider," and Frank White. A preliminary deposit of $100 was put up for each man. DULUTH, MINN., Aug. 7.—The Canadian tug James H. Walker was fined $250 here yesterday for towing in American waters. She arrived Monday night towning the schooner Brandon. Prisoner Taken to Goshen to Avoid Mob of Lynchers.
GOSHEN, Aug. 3.—[Special.]—Ben Scott of Elkhart was brought here this evening by a strong guard and lodged in jail. He is charged with the murder of Con Crowley at Elkhart. It seems he and three other men became engaged in a quarrel in a butcher's shop there, when Scott pulled out a long knife and stabbed all the other three men, saying as he killed Crowley, "Lay there, you d—d scoundrel; all I want is your money." The knife went to the heart, penetrating over four inches. The other two men were not seriously hurt. After the stabbing, Scott started on a run and managed to get three miles into the country before he was caught. In the meantime a posse was formed for the purpose of lynching him and had started in pursuit, but missed the officers, who came straight here with the prisoner. Fears are entertained here of an attempt to enter the jail by Crowley's Elkhart friends who are thirsting for Scott's blood. The jail has a strong guard about it to-night.

JACKSON, Miss., Aug. 14.—A fatal shooting affray, closely followed by a lynching, is reported from the village of Utica, Miss., 35 miles west of here. The following account of the tragedy has been received: On Sunday evening E. B. Robertson, a young white man, was conducting a young lady to church. They were met on the sidewalk by Bob Broom, colored, with several colored girls. Broom refused to yield any portion of the sidewalk, and rudely pushed Robertson to one side. The latter told the negro that he would see him again. After church Robertson was standing in front of a store explaining the occurrence to several friends, when Broom with four companions came up and commenced firing upon the white men, who were unarmed. STURLING, NEB., Aug. 14.—Saturday night Lettle Walker, the 7-year-old daughter of H. N. Walker, was shot by her father, who mistook her for a burglar. Indignant Citizens Avenge the Crime Under Judge Lynch's Code.

JACKSON, MISS., Aug. 13.—At Utica, in this county, last night Beverly Robinson (white), while escorting a young lady from church, was met by Bob Broom, a negro, who was accompanied by some negro girls. Broom and his companions took the sidewalk, forcing Robinson and his lady into the street.

About 11 o'clock, two hours after the occurrence, Robinson and several friends were discussing the matter, when Broom and several other negroes approached and opened fire, instantly killing Dr. Holliday and wounding Frank Wallace and Armond White.

The attack was so sudden that no resistance was made by the whites. An investigation to-day proved Broom's guilt, and this evening he was taken from jail by a mob of 200 men and hanged in the cemetery yard. His accomplices escaped, but men are searching for them. Great excitement prevails.

Places Another Victim on His List.

An Impudent and Brutal Negro
Hanged at Utica, Miss.

Special Dispatch to The Appeal.
JACKSON, Miss., Aug. 13. — Utica, a flourishing and enterprising town some thirty-five miles below here, on the Natchez, Jackson & Columbus railroad, was the scene last night and today of two tragedies, with great excitement attendant thereon. Last night a young gentleman, Mr. Beverly Robinson, while conducting a young lady to church, was met on the sidewalk by a negro named Bob Broom with some colored girls, who refused to give any of the way. Mr. Robinson politely asked them to give the way, when Broom cursed him and said he would not, and at the same time rudely pushed the young lady with whom Robinson was walking off the pavement. Robinson offered no resistance at the time, but told him he would see him again, and each party left.

At 11:30 o'clock on the same night Robinson and Frank Wallace were standing on the street in front of a store talking when they were joined by Dr. L. W. Holliday, a practicing physician in Utica. Soon thereafter the aforesaid Bob Broom with four other negroes came up, and, without warning or provocation, commenced shooting into the crowd. Dr. Holliday was shot through the head, his brains oozing out of the wound. Robinson caught Broom from behind and held him till he had emptied his pistol. There was no shooting done by the whites. Frank Wallace drew his pistol, but before he could fire it he was shot through the arm by Broom and disabled. Armand White was seriously shot through the thigh. The negro Broom was arrested on the spot, his companions and accomplices fled.

There was a legal investigation of the case held at Utica this morning, in which the foregoing facts were elicited, after which an angry crowd of citizens of over 200, being determined to avenge the diabolical outrage, took Broom to the cemetery on the edge of the town and hung him. This occurred between 4 and 5 o'clock this evening. Utica and the surrounding country is peopled by the most law abiding, peaceable and enlightened citizens that we have in the State, but they are not the sort to brook outrages of this kind without avenging them. Ike Broom and Sam Harris were also arrested and are now in the Raymond jail, but there is no evidence against them, and they have shown they were only lookers on. Raney Short and Curtis Short escaped. Broom, the negro who was hung, said Curtis did some of the shooting. A posse is after them. They are supposed to have gone to Vicksburg.

SLAIN BY AN UNKNOWN.
Frank Dodge, of Morton, Mysteriously Murdered at Redwood Falls.
Frank Dodge, of Morton, Mysteriously Murdered at Redwood Falls.

Special to the Globe.

REDWOOD FALLS, Minn., Nov. 24.—The peaceful village of Redwood Falls was startled early this morning by the report that a man had been murdered in cold blood during the night. A party of young people returning from a dance at Delhi saw what they supposed to be a drunken man lying by the roadside in one of the principal streets. On investigating they were horrified to find that the man was dead and with a bullet hole through his head. The murdered man's name was Frank Dodge, a barber from Morton, Renville county. Last evening he drove to Redwood Falls with his cousin, the latter intending to take the Northwestern train for Rochester this morning. The cousin retired at the Exchange hotel soon after 9 o'clock, while Dodge was about town till late and was seen in a saloon between 10 and 11 o'clock. When or where he was killed is unknown. Death was caused by a bullet from a 32-calibre revolver entering the head at the middle of the base of the skull and lodging in the brain. When found the body was lying face downward, the face being in a small pool of blood. Fresh wagon tracks were discovered near the corpse, and this with other signs indicates that Dodge was shot and conveyed in a wagon to the spot where his body was found and dumped out. A watch was found on the body but no money. Several persons have been under surveillance to-day, but there is scarcely any clue to follow up. All that is definitely known is that Dodge had paid attention to a waitress at the Exchange hotel some time since. It is thought that there is some woman at the bottom of the tragedy. The inquest is in progress. Deceased was about twenty-five years old and unmarried.

Prisoners Are Removed to a Place of Safety to Escape a Mob.
of Safety to Escape a Mob.

Special to the Globe.

REDWOOD FALLS, Minn., Nov. 26.—The town has been in a ferment all day over the mysterious murder of Frank Dodge Friday night. This crime, together with the acquittal of a murderer here some three years ago and the light sentence of six years' imprisonment just imposed upon Gorres for murdering Rosenkranz, and the probability of a disagreement of the jury in the Rose murder case, aroused the citizens of the town and county to a high pitch of indignation. Morton people were terribly wrought up over the Dodge murder and Sheriff Mead was warned this forenoon to look out for trouble to-night-Acting upon this hint he took Holden, the man arrested for the murder of Dodge, to jail at New Ulm at 4:10 this afternoon. Rose was also taken along, as the jury this forenoon was discharged, having failed to agree after being out over sixty hours. The lock-up here is a frail wooden structure, and a mob would have made short work with it. There is not doubt that Holden would have been lynched to-night had he remained here, and Rose's chances would not have been much better.

Holden signed an affidavit this morning, the substance of which was that while driving from Morton, Dodge shot himself about one mile east of town, and that Holden brought the body in and placed it where it was found. Holden says he hid $70 in money in the bed at the Exchange on Friday night, and that it was his own money. The roll of bills was found as indicated. Holden tells numerous differing stories, and is very nervous, so that the opinion is universal that he shot Dodge. The motive is unknown, but is supposed to have been robbery, as the roll of bills, undoubtedly, belonged to Dodge. The verdict of the coroner's jury charges Holden with the murder. So far as known, Holden and Dodge had always been on good terms.

Severe Electric Storm in Ithaca. ITHACA, June 11.—An unusually severe thunder shower visited this region of central New York about 9 o'clock last evening. The storm moved from the north. A fine residence near Aurora, owned and occupied by Mr. Beatty, was struck by lightning and entirely consumed. The storm was noticed to be especially terrific on the west side of the lake, and much damage was done in its course. It had lost none of its fury when it burst over this city. The lightning was blindingly vivid and almost instantaneous, with deafening thunder. The electric light wires were struck by the first bolt, and the lights went out with a pop. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western depot was also struck and set on fire by the lightning, as was the residence of Irving W. Stout on North Cayuga street. Lynch Law in Florida.
ELLAVILLE, Fla., June 11.—On Saturday night Superintendent William McCormick was shot by Dennis Williams, colored, through the right shoulder, the bullet smashing a bone and working its way through the back. McCormick ordered Dennis to deliver a gun to him which he carried against orders. Dennis told McCormick to stand back, and when McCormick again demanded the gun Dennis fired. He was pursued and caught, and was locked up in a smoke-house, which was closely guarded. Early yesterday morning his guards were found gagged and bound, and the house empty. It was thought that Williams's friends had released him, but this morning Williams's body was found in the Suwanee River riddled with bullets and his head badly smashed.

The Victim of Her Husband's Abuse.

GAINESVILLE, Texas, June 11.—At Sunset, near here yesterday, Dr. Wiley, a physician, stripped his wife of all her clothing, and beat her unmercifully. She escaped from him and ran through the streets in an entirely nude condition. The doctor pursued her, firing at her from his revolver, but failed to hit her. She sought refuge in a neighbor's house, where the doctor, on attempting to enter, was disarmed and handed over to the authorities. He was taken to the Montague jail to prevent lynching by the infuriated citizens. Mrs. Wiley, who is a most estimable lady, will die from the effects of beating and kicks.

Dynamite in a Barrel of Fish.

DETROIT, June 11.—A barrel of fish, in which was a dynamite bomb, was a part of the cargo in the hold of the steamer City of Cleveland on her trip from Cleveland on last Wednesday. The barrel was one of a number consigned by John Kingsboro, a wholesale fish dealer at Cleveland, to Ryan & Bourke of this city. The bomb was discovered when the barrel was opened the following day, and was thrown into the river. From the appearance of the barrel it had been opened and the bomb placed in it after the barrel had left the warehouse in Cleveland.

Lynched a Colored Soldier.

HELENA. Mont., June 11.—Robertson, a negro soldier at Fort Shaw, on Saturday night had a row with a man near the fort over a disreputable woman, and killed an innocent bystander. Fifty masked citizens from Sun River took the man out last night and lynched him.

Seventeen-year Locusts Coming. CHICAGO, June 12.—Despatches from northern Iowa and western Illinois report the appearance of swarms of seventeen-year locusts. Prof. C. V. Riley, United States Entomologist, who is at present in Chicago, says the visitors may be looked for in wooded portions of Illinois and Iowa, and also, as indicated by the experience of 1871, in the northwest counties of Wisconsin, extending as far south as the Kankakee River; in the southern tier of Michigan counties, extending from Lake Michigan east to the middle of the State, and in Lancaster county, Penn, and the southeast portion of the State known as the "Pequea valley." He has just received a telegram that the young are hatching in immense numbers in parts of Minnesota, and, with favorable weather to them, considerable injury may be done. He thinks they will never do as much injury as they did between the years 1873 and 1877. Killed by His Fifteen-Year-Old Son. BALTIMORE, June 12.—Peter Alt, proprietor of the Arlington House, was shot and almost instantly killed last night by his son William, aged 15 years. The shooting took place in the kitchen. Alt's wife says the shooting was done in her defence. Her husband had been on a spree for some time, and just before the tragedy he came into the house, and after breaking a heavy cup and saucer on her head, began to beat her. She struggled with him and they both fell on the floor. He got a hold on her throat, and she thought that he meant to kill her. She was almost insensible when she heard the report of a gun. Her husband's grip on her throat relaxed and he fell over on the floor. Young Alt, who is a bright looking boy, was arrested and locked up after an affectionate parting with his mother. Escape of a Female Convict.
ANAMOSEE, Ia., June 12.—Anna L. Hower, a female convict, made her escape from the penitentiary here on Sunday night by sawing off an iron bar over her window in the top tier of cells and letting herself down by means of bed clothes, then climbing up a rope and scaling the wall. She was sent from Cedar Rapids for eighteen years for murder in the second degree, she having assisted a man in killing her husband. She afterward ran away with her paramour. She had served five years. She is the first female that has ever escaped.

Lynched a Colored Criminal.

TALLAHASSA, Fla., June 12.—Dennis Williams, colored, who shot and seriously wounded Superintendent McCormack at Ellerville on Saturday, was taken to the woods by a mob and lynched yesterday. His body was afterward found in the river. The negroes are greatly incensed, and it is reported they will try to avenge the lynching.

Matricide Hawkins's Uncle Insane.

Islip, June 12.—Francis Asbury Clock, the uncle and godfather of Francis Asbury Hawkins, now in the Riverhead jail for the murder of his mother, has become insane. He had been considered eccentric. When he saw the dead body of his sister and awoke to the fact that his namesake was a matricide he received a shock from which he never recovered. A family consultation was held lately, and his brothers, H. T., L. D., and N. Oakley Clock called in Dr. Gunn of New York. By Dr. Gunn's advice he was removed to a private asylum. It is believed that his malady is the result of brooding over the impending fate of his nephew.
