The Pope's expenses last year were $1,-400,000, his income from Peter's Pence was $1,425,000.

The centennial of Alexander Campbell's birth will be celebrated at Bethany College, June 21.

Bishop Gilmour has ordered that no priest shall officiate at any funeral where flowers are displayed.

The fifty-first session of the General Association of Baptists in Kentucky will be held at Eminence, June 20.

The meeting at Midway Baptist Church closed with forty-three additions—twenty-four by baptism and nineteen by letter.

According to last year's count, church membership in this nation is as follows: Congregationalists, 436,379; Presbyterians, (North and South), 847,165; Lutherans, 981,616; Baptists, 2,917,315; Methodists, (North and South), 3,144,466.

Methodists are pleased with the plan of the General Conference to make the order of programme of service uniform the country over. The order adopted is: Singing, all standing; prayer, minister and all kneeling; lesson from both Old and New Testaments; hymn, standing; preaching; prayer, all kneeling; collection; benediction.—Exchange.

LYNCHED A FLORIDA NEGRO.
Dennis Williams Hanged by a Mob for Wounding a White Man.
Dennis Williams, the colored man who shot Superintendent McCormick at Ella-ville. Fla., a lumber depot some thirty miles east of Tallahassee, was lynched and his body found in the Suwanee River. The guards who were left in charge of the negro were bound hand and foot by the lynchers. The shooting was caused by an attempt of the superintendent of the mills to make Williams deliver up a loaded gun which he had and held in a threatening manner in a crowd of people. Williams refused to do so, and then McCormick attempted to take the gun, and Williams fired a charge into McCormick's shoulder, shattering the bone. McCormick is very popular, and the shooting created immense excitement. Since the finding of Williams' body, it is rumored that the negroes have banded together for revenge.

THE WEST.

Fire the other night destroyed the works of the Indianapolis Veneer Company and the fancy cabinet ware factory of D. E. Stone & Co. The aggregate loss was about $100,000, with $53,500 insurance.

During a storm recently lightning struck the house of Beerlet Gunderson, living four miles south of Clarkfield, Minn., and killed two children and shocked the remainder of the family severely.

The three-mile race between Kennedy, of Quincy, Ill., and Plaisted, of Portland, Me., on Lake Quinsingamond was easily won by the former, who took the lead at the start and finished thirty lengths ahead in 22 minutes, $7½ seconds.

A rabid cur created a great disturbance in the Town of Lake, near Chicago, the other evening, biting several men and children, besides a number of dogs and horses, before the police succeeded in killing him. Two of the children bitten were terribly lacerated.

POLICE OFFICER TIMOTHY SULLIVAN, who was one of the detail which stood the damage of the Anarchist bomb at Chicago, May 4, 1886, died recently. He received a bullet in the thigh, and the blood poisoning which supervened gradually sapped his strength until death ensued.

A CLAY bank in a brick yard at Menominee, Minn., caved in the other morning. Beneath it were seven men. Two brothers named James were taken out dead and terribly mangled. Ole Holte and Ole Hecker lived only a few hours. Knute Knutson, Ben Farmstad and Nels Swenson had broken legs or arms and received internal injuries.

NINETEEN persons were poisoned at Kassola, Minn., recently by eating poisoned cheese, which was found to have been manufactured in Wisconsin. Many of the victims became insensible after suffering spasms, but all recovered.

The sixth annual convention of the Missouri Woman's Christian Temperance Union commenced at Kansas City on the 13th.

SOLOMON G. COMSTOCK has been nominated for Congress, to succeed Knute Nelson, by the Republicans of the Fifth Minnesota district.

WALTER L. HAYES has been renominated for Congress by the Democrats of the Second Iowa district.

The negroes of the Chickasaw Nation are making elaborate preparations for a general exodus to Oklahoma, where they contemplate farming. Numerous colonies are entering lands and making permanent homes. Sam Paul, a full-blooded Chickasaw Tribal Senator, is assisting the colored people in this move.

RECENTLY published statistics of the Chicago Union Stock Yards Company, and of the Chicago Board of Trade, show that the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy railroad is still leading all other lines in the number of cars of live stock and grain brought to that market. This fact indicates the rapidity with which the road must have recovered from its recent labor troubles, and furnishes additional evidence of the efficient manner in which the management handled the recent strikes of employees on its lines. Evidently, from a business standpoint, the road is in able hands.

A heavy wind storm passed over Tiffin, O., the other morning, blowing down the wal's of the Beaver Falls glass factory and gas well derricks. Thousands of dollars of damage was done to fruit and grain.

A curious fact has developed in the Prohibition nomination for Governor of Missouri. The nominee, Frank M. Lowe, of Kansas City, is only twenty-eight years old, when the law requires the Governor to be at least thirty.
THE Supreme Lodge Knights of Pythias, at Cincinnati on the 14th, elected the following officers: Supreme chancellor, William Ward, of Newark, N. J.; supreme vice-chancellor, George D. Shaw, of Eau Claire, Wis.; supreme prelate, Charles T. Bragg, of Bangor, Me.; supreme keeper of the records and seals, R. M. C. White, of Nashville, Tenn.; supreme master of arms, Robert Newell, of Little Rock; supreme outer guard, John W. Thompson, of Washington; supreme master of the exchequer, Stansberry J. Willey, of Wilmington, Del.

Miss Mollie Garfield, daughter of the murdered President, was married to J. Stanley Brown at Mentor, O., on the 14th. At the same time and place, Henry Garfield, Mollie's brother, was married to Miss Belle Mason, daughter of the late Hon. James Mason, of Cleveland. The wedding was a quiet affair, newspaper men being excluded.

An electric storm played havoc at Milwaukee, Wis., on the 14th. The telegraph and telephone systems were greatly damaged. In Cheboygan County a farmer named Cooper was killed by lightning.

The International Typographical Union, lately in session at Kansas City, elected Edwin T. Plank, of San Francisco, president. The new constitution provides for biennial meetings.

A DISPATCH from Superior, Wis., of the 14th says the damage by the floods in Northern Minnesota would amount to $500,000. The boom at Cloquet gave way, causing the loss of several million feet of logs.

THE SOUTH.

General Felix C. Agnus, publisher of the American, has undertaken the task of raising $500,000 for the erection of an exposition building in Baltimore, Md.

THE six days' walking match for women, came to a close at Baltimore, Md., on the 9th. The finish was very exciting. The score was: Tobias, 315; Cleveland, 313; Kilbury, 303; Macbeth, 275.

THE other night nine miles south of Longview, Tex., in a difficulty about a trivial matter, Walter Roson, aged eighteen, shot and killed Fletcher Welch, an old man.

DENNIS WILLIAMS, colored, who shot and seriously wounded Superintendent McCormick at Tallahassee, Fla., recently, was taken to the woods by a mob and lynched.

A quarrel between John Dunn and John Culverson in Lee County, Ala., a few evinings since, culminated in a duel with pocket-knives, in which Culverson's throat was cut, resulting in his death in a short time. Dunn was badly cut about the ace, and may not recover.

The cotton product of the levee district in Mississippi last year was 140,930 bales.

A family quarrel resulted in the murder of Jesse J. Marlow at Ocala, Fla., a few days ago, by a neighbor named Green Hodge.

W. T. Wilson, a well-known business man of Atlanta, Ga., committed suicide a few days ago by taking strychnine.

Charles Murphy, a fisherman, while drawing in his net near Louisville, Ky., a few days ago, was dragged under the water and drowned.

The strawberry season in Tennessee is over.

The city of Columbus, Miss., by an almost unanimous vote favored a subscription of $80,000 to the Memphis, Oxford & Columbus railroad. Work is in progress at Columbus on the western extension of the Georgia Pacific railway.

W. A. Elliott, aged twenty-one, and Miss Maggie Stewart, aged eighteen, were out driving at Childersburg, Ala., a few days ago, when the horse took fright and ran into the river, drowning both the young man and young lady.

Convicts to the number of eighteen, employed on the Versailles, Midway & Georgetown railroad, escaped from their camp, near Georgetown, Ky., a few nights ago, and at last accounts were still at large. A reward of $50 each is offered for their capture.

Captain John J. Brown, a well-known steamboat man, died at New Orleans a few days since.

J. B. Friedman, a merchant of Boutte, La., and railroad express agent at that place, which is on the Morgan railroad, was shot in the back, a few nights ago, by an unknown person and died a few hours later. The assassin escaped.

The National organization of the colored Y. M. C. A. was completed at Louisville, Ky., by the election of Chas. S. Morris president; W. H. Goodall, Albert Mack, L. W. Cross and W. C. Duson, vicepresidents; Albert White, secretary, and G. W. Talbott, treasurer. Morris is only thirty-eight years old. He has been a teacher in the Louisville public schools, has just finished a course at Howard College, Washington, D. C., and intends to go to Harvard. His mother is a public-school teacher in Louisville.

J. T. Shepherd, a railroad post-office clerk of the New Orleans & Marshall railroad post-office, was arrested a few days ago charged with embezzling registered mail letters. The arrest is considered one of the most important made in some time, as the theft involves something over $1,000. There were five packages taken, one alone containing $515. This package was a remittance from the postmaster at Donaldsonville, La., to the New Orleans post-office.

Governor Buckner of Kentucky has refused to commute the sentence of Wm. Patterson, who is to be hanged in Louisville on the 22d for participation in the murder of Jennie Bowman.

As Turnkey James Turner of the Henderson (Ky.) jail was entering the building with the dinner of the prisoners a few days ago, one of them, named Baxter, jumped upon him and tried to knock him down. Turner drew his revolver and shot Baxter fatally, but in the meantime three of the prisoners had made good their escape.

The negro miners at Warrior, Ala., for some supposed offense of the white bosses, recently armed themselves with the intention of killing the first white man who molests them. The white men decided on the same course, and blood-shed seemed imminent.

Wm. J. Palmer died at the Morgantown (N. C.) Insane Asylum a few days since from injuries inflicted by an inmate of the institution. Mr. Palmer was a graduate of Columbia College and had been super-intendent of a number of insane asylums until he went insane himself.

A special train on the East Tennessee, Virginia & Georgia railway, carrying Jay Gould and party, made the fastest time on record in the South a few days since. The distance from Chattanooga to Knoxville, 112 miles, was made in two hours and seventeen minutes, which included two stops of five minutes each.

The trustees of the University of Tennessee have elected Charles E. Wait, of Rolla, Mo., to the chair of chemistry and metallurgy; Thomas L. Norwood, of Bingham School, N. C., professor of modern languages; Wm. W. Carson, professor of mathematics, and Thomas C. Karns, associate professor of the English language.

Alfred Blackwell, of Barclaysville, N. C., was found dead at his saw-mill, a few nights ago, being most fearfully mutilated! He had been trying to run his saw-mill alone, and it is supposed accidentally fell on the saw, when he suffered a most shocking death. His left arm was severed in two places, and his body was completely cut in twain except at the spinal column.

The Louisiana Senate confirmed the nomination of ex-Governor McEnery to be Associate Justice of the Supreme Court for the term of twelve years, in place of Robert B. Todd, whose term has just expired.

Oscar Searcy was killed at Greenville, Ala., a few nights ago, by a shot accidentally fired by Webb Perdue, who was flourishing a weapon in a reckless manner while under the influence of liquor.

W. H. Remert, a wealthy planter, residing in Sumter County, S. C., was recently sentenced to two years' hard labor for persisting in consorting with a negress to the utter neglect of his young and beautiful wife. His colored companion received a like sentence.

Dennis Williams, colored, was lynched at Ellaville, Fla., a few days since the crime of shooting at a white man. His body was found in the Suwannee river, perforated with bullets and having a rope around the neck.

Sam Jones' brother has eloped.

A sensation was created at Holly Springs, Miss., recently, by the conversion of Thomas F. Seligman, a saloon-keeper, who displayed a sign across his door "Closed for Good." This is one of the results of a Methodist revival, conducted by Rev. George S. Inge, under which many conversions have been made.

An Americus (Ga.) gentleman has a lot of young 'possums and kittens which he is raising together as a "happy family."

Two large bears have been committing depredations in Whitefield County, Ga., recently, and have thus far managed to elude the hunting parties organized for their destruction.

Birmingham (Ala.) bootblacks pay a license of ten dollars a year.

Robert Bratcher was recently tried at Abbeville, S. C., for enticing away a laborer under contract, a serious offense in that State. He wooed and won Miss Hamilton, the laborer in question, and married her, taking her to his home, hence the suit. The jury was disposed to be lenient, however, and returned a verdict of not guilty.

DETROIT, Jan. 31.—The number of cocking mains in and about Detroit recently have stirred up the police to extraordinary activity and vigilance, and as a result the saloon of Pat Joy, at Michigan avenue and Third street, was raided at 3 a. m. and nine men arrested. A main was in full blast, and a lot of birds were captured. The doors had to be forced. Two of the crowd got upstalrs, and, running over the roof of another building, escaped. The others were pulled from their hiding places and driven to the Central station.

Excited Over an Absent Negro.

WINCHESTER, O., Jan. 31.—Great excitement prevails here over the flight of Dick Dent, colored, for whose arrest a warrant was sworn out Tuesday morning by Miss Jennie Darlington, a pretty farmer's daughter, only sixteen, charging him with seduction. She first secured a warrant for an innocent school teacher named Nichols, but soon confessed she had done it under threats of violence from Dent. If the negro is caught he will be lynched. The white population are all out searching for the fugitive.

Sentenced for Dueling.

GREENVILLE, Tex., Jau. 31.—Andrew J. Beason and W. P. Mills, both young men and living in this county, on the 12th of November last engaged in a sort of a mutual combat with pistols within about six feet of each other. Fortunately neither of the parties were hit. Beason was tried in the district court for assault to murder on Mills, and the jury at a late hour Saturday night returned a verdict of guilty with two years in the penitentiary. The other party, W. P. Mills, is also indicted for the same offense committed on Beason.

An Insane Girl Shoots Herself.

TAYLORVILLE, Ill., Jan. 31. — Miss Roxie Revel, a demented girl, living with her parents, Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Revel, living near this city, attempted suicide. She got hold of a revolver and fired two shots, the first taking effect in her right temple. Medical aid was summoned, but it is thought she will die. About five years ago she was sent to the asylum at Jacksonville, where she remained six months.

Stolen Silver Bricks Recovered.

LAKE VALLEY, N. M., Jan. 31.—The Silver Mining company made a lucky find of three silver bricks, worth several thousand dollars. These bricks are a part of several hundred thousand dollars worth of bullion stolen from the Bridal Chamber mine four years ago. They were found among the debris of the old smelter.

Disastrous Explosion.
PITTSBURG, Feb. 1.—A Gallitzin, Pa., special says: A terrible explosion occurred in a house on Portage street last evening, by which four men were hurt, two of whom cannot recover. It was in a Polish boarding house. The explosion was caused by a spark from a lighted cigar dropping into a can of blasting powder which the men were working with. The house was entirely demolished. All of the injured are seriously hurt, and two only have any chance for recovery.

Reduction of Ten Per Cent. in Wages.

PITTSBURG, Feb. 1.—A general reduction of ten per cent. in the wages of the employes of the Cambria, at Johnstown, Pa., went into effect today. The works are running as usual in all departments but the wire mill. These men are now holding a meeting with closed doors. No trouble is anticipated by the company. Upwards of 10,000 men are employed in the works and mines.

Was It Foul Play?

PITTSBURG, Feb. 1.—A Somerset (Pa.) special says: Rev. Cornelius Birkley, an aged minister of the German Baptist church, was yesterday found dead in a field on his farm, half way between a country road and his house. He had started the night before to walk home. Not reaching home, search was made, which resulted in finding the lifeless body lying face downward in the snow.

Lee Pleads Guilty.

CHICAGO, Feb. 1.—Mrs. Rawson, wife of Banker Rawson, and her son, William Ralph Lee, were brought into Judge Clifford's court today, to answer to the charges preferred against them. Young Lee pleaded guilty of an assault with intent to kill, and was remanded to jail.

He Breathes the Free Air Again.

DUBLIN, Feb. 1.—Ex-Lord Mayor Sullivan, of Dublin, was released from Tullamore prison today, after two months' confinement. A large crowd was gathered in front of the building and greeted Mr. Sullivan with great enthusiasm.

More Trouble Abroad.

CONSTANTINOPLE, Feb. 1.—It is reported here that two more Russian raids upon Bulgaria are being prepared. The Somalia have murdered an English officer and twenty-three natives of Berbera.

Cox Gets One Month.

DUBLIN, Feb. 1.—Cox, the convicted member of parliament, for making a speech in October, inciting tenants to conspiracy, was sentenced to one month's imprisonment.

Particulars of the Lynching of a Rapist In Mississippi—A Queer Character.

Memphis, July 19.—(Special.)—Miss Amelia Shives, the victim of the imposter, George H. Thomas, who was hanged and shot full of holes near Oxford, Miss., three days ago, has been completely prostrated since the unfortunate occurrence and her physicians consider her condition rather critical. She is held blameless and entirely free from wrong by every good citizen of the county. Expressions of sympathy are given her from everywhere, and indignation at the wrong done her knows no bounds. It was not until today that the details of the crime, already briefly outlined by your correspondent, could be obtained. The case is one of the most sensational, in many respects, which has occurred in North Mississippi for years.

Thomas did not go to his fate bravely, as every indication showed that he became helpless and had to be dragged the last hundred yards. His form was well proportioned. He was five feet eleven inches high and weighed 225 pounds. He presented a magnificent front with massive brows, piercing gray eyes, and wore a seven and one half hat. He was about forty-five years of age, and his silver locks reached almost to his shoulders. His address was most impressive and attractive and his influence over people was most powerful. He carried no baggage but claimed every day to be expecting a trunk full of clothing and had Mr. Shives send in his wagon for it. He said the trunk would not only have clothing, but documents bearing upon the history of the world, which he claimed to be writing. After his arrest, it was discovered that although his feet were not larger than a No. 4 shoe, he wore a No. 7 stuffed with cotton to make it fit. To-day the Sheriff found in the lining of his coat eight kinds of ladies' hair and three varieties of wigs and false beard. He is said to have had several diamonds, which he claimed to be worth $1,000 apiece. He had just enough money to pay his board. He came to Mr. Shrives' from the western part of the county afoot, claiming that he had traveled on foot more than twenty-two years, never traveling any other way. He would never come to Oxford himself, saying that he would prefer to wait until his better clothes should come. Mr. Shives' family were impressed with his extreme goodness and piety, and he was at once requested to ask a table blessing and then to lead in family prayer, all of which he did with such devoutness and spirit that he had the entire confidence of the family. Learning that Miss Shives was afflicted, he very kindly offered his services gratis, claiming to be a physician by education and by some practice. Miss Shives took his medicine, which he always carried, and from that time forward he spent more time with her.

His influence over her began to assert itself and increase until the final dose of medicine was given on last Saturday, when his control over her was absolute. She was mesmerized, drugged and outraged.

Oxford, Miss., July 17.—For a month past a man claiming to be Dr. G. H. Thomas, whose occupation was a world’s historian, besides being a physician and Christian gentleman, has peen stopping at Mr. Allen Shives', a farmer living ten miles east of this point.

While there he won the complete confidence of the family, and Miss Amelis Shives, a cultured lady about 35 years of age, but who was in poor health, was persuaded to undergo his secret treatment.

By dint of wiles and drugs Thomas managed to accomplish her ruin last Saturday. About 1 o'clock last night Thomas who had been arrested, was taken from the constable guard by a mob of about fifty men from the east and hanged. His body was riddled with bullets.

Philadelphia Church 15 Miles East of Oxford, July. 30, 1888

|We publish the following proceedings as a public newspaper and because 104 citizens of the county have made a personal request to that effect who by their signatures assume the responsibility for what they have said. No one shall have cause to complain of any publication of our own about any matter if we know it. Whereas, we have heard of the wilful and malicious lynching of a man known as Dr. Thomas, in the neighborhood of Pine Hill church, some eight or ten miles north-east of Oxford, without cause or provocation, one of the most outrageous and brutal known of in this country. we therefore here express our disapproval and condemnation of all such acts and think that the same ought to be immediately investigated and we here express our willingness to assist in said investigation, and we therefore personally request the proper authorities to proceed at once to said investigation and we, believing as we do with the light before us in the case that the guilty ones can be found and believing it to be the duty of every good citizen to see that the law is executed, we personally request every good citizen that is opposed to all such lawlessness to join us and see that persons guilty of such a deed are punished.

Resolved, that the Secretary copy the proceedings of this meeting and send one copy to the county paper and one to the Courier-Journal for publication.
dr-g-h-thomas-1888-07-16.A6:
To the Public.
As one of the guards of Dr. Thomas who was taken by a mob on the 16th of July, and shot, I desire to make a statment of my connection with the unfortunate affair, that I may not be misjudged or misrepresented. On Monday evening the 16th, while on my way to church a negro handed me a note from Sheriff Mattlews asking me to go to the house where Dr. Thomas was under arrest and guard him that night. After the services at the church, I went to the place as requested by the Sheriff. I suppose it was ten o'clock when I got there. I found Mr. James Matthews, a nephew of the sheriff's, there to assist me in guarding the prisoner, who had demanded a trial and which was to be had next day before Esquire Smith, the magistrate in that Beat. The prisoner was chained to a wagon under a large tree in the yard and made perfectly comfortable. He was offered food at meal time and treated as well as any prisoner could be. About two o'clock at night while the prisoner slept and Matthews and I were on guard a crowd of men numbering six or seven, surrounded us and at the point of the pistol I was searched and ordered to leave. The prisoner was tied with a plow line and hurried away and soon after I heard shots in the direction where his body was found next day. I had no thought of there being a mob and was consequently taken by surprise. Messrs James Matthews, Clayton Shive and myself went to Mr. Dave Butler's residence, about four hundred yards from Mr. Shives, and told him a mob had taken the prisoner. We did this because we wanted some disinterested party to know about the matter at once. I do not know anything about who composed the mob, as I did recognize any of them. I certainly would have prevented the killing of the prisoner if I could have done so, and I am also satisfied that Mr. Matthews, cur sheriff, had no intention of mob violence or he would have taken the prisoner to jail at Oxford. The reason the prisoner was not taken away was, that he demanded a trial and it had to be had there because some of the witnesses were so feeble they could not go to Oxford, which is ten miles away. I went the next day and helped to find and bury the body. I write this because I understand there are some parties disposed to consure the guards and to implicate them with at least a knowledge of the unfortunate affair. So far as I am concerned I would not have been there without more guards had I had any idea that he would have been taken by a mob. There was no threats of violence in that neighborhood and the sheriff had no intimation that anything of the sort would be attempted. As an evidence of this the sheriff put his nephew as one of only two guards over the prisoner. No one in the whole community so far as I know had any idea of such a thing and it is unjust to the sheriff to think that he expected it.

M. HAWKINS

e-langley-jones-colorado-city.A1:
NEARLY LYNCHED.
How a Man was Mistaken for a Horse-Thief-What Came of It.
to Colorado City from my ranche in Tom Green county, Texas, as was my custom at least once a month for the purpose of getting my mail and ordering supplies for the ranche. While I was making preparations for the long ride back of seventy miles, the Sheriff of the county came over to the corral to inform me, that seeing one of my cowponies in a "bunch" that had been driven into town the day before for shipment, he had impounded it until my arrival. This delayed my getting off until about two hours before sundown, but, as I had calculated that the moon would be up about 8 o'clock, I determined to push, on and according set out leading my recovered horse. As ill luck would have it, I had not gone more than nine or ten miles before I discovered that in my hurry of departure I had forgotten a bottle of medicine which I had promised to get for one of the boys, and I concluded to go back for it. I thereupon hitched my lead horse to a mesquite bush, and, setting spurs to my trusty pony, "loped" all the way back. On calling for my bottle I was told by the jovial drug-store clerk that a posse from Scurry county was out hunting horse thieves, expressing a hope that I might strike their camp, to all of which I paid little or no attention. By this time of course it was almost pitch dark, and I jogged along unconsciously, leaving the road entirely to the pony, who I knew would not lead me astray, and as I reached the place where my other horse was tied I would have passed it had he not whinnied. Throwing the lines over my pony's head I dismounted, and, having unhitched the other pony from the bush, was just about to tie him to the horn of the saddle, when a gruff voice thundered out: "Throw up your hands, or by — you're a dead man!" I was completely taken by surprise and a sudden fear possessed me almost to paralization. The next moment the cold muzzle of a Colt's "44" was placed against my temple with the unnecessary warning that if I moved a muscle I would be blown to Hades. Not very gently my hands were tied behind my back and I was ordered to mount my horse. This, of course, was an utter impossibility without help, and I got it with a vengeance. I was collared and kicked and then thrown across the saddle like a sack of barley. The lariat with which my hands were tied was then attached to the horn of one of my captor's saddle, and with the other in front we rode in single file towards the town. What their feelings were I do not, and probably never shall know, but for my own, were I to live to be a hundred years old I steadfastly believe the horrors of that ride will be as vivid as they are today. For the benefit of those who are not aware of the fact it may be stated that the stealing of horses or cattle in the wild southwest is deemed worthy of the death penalty. No mercy is shown the horse thief, and if not lynched he is often "ear-marked" by having the tips of his ears sliced off before imprisonment. On nearing town my power of speech to some extent returned to me, and I began to question them as to their authority for arresting me. This was met with the crushing reply that they would show me their authority when they reached the next cross-bar. The cross-bar is a beam over a cattle gate, generally about ten feet from the ground, used as a safeguard against the spreading outwards of the gate posts, and was a favorite place for lynching horsethieves. As I knew that there was no gate to be encountered until we reached the town itself, I began to feel a little more confident, and endeavored to explain matters; but to no purpose. On reaching town my two captors decided to keep me until the rest of the gang should return from the chase, so that they also might enjoy the felicity of seeing me "strung up," and I was accordingly taken into a saloon in the lower end of town, where I was unfortunately unknown, and my "friends" proceeded to make merry over their huge fortune in catching the "little horse-stealing puppy," or words to that effect. I must here state that during all this time neither of them had once looked at the brands of my horses; and I now asked them what brand the horses that had been stolen were marked with. The bigger of the two replied with numberless oaths that they "were onto that racket. You can't fool us like that, young feller; it doesn't take long to change a brand like our," and so forth, until I began to fear that after all I might be lynched before any of my friends in town got wind of it. However, shortly after the rest of the posse came in, and among them was one whom I at once recognized as an Englishman by his wearing kneebreeches and cavalry spurs, and signaling him to step aside, I managed to whisper that I was a countryman of his and that I was entirely innocent. On his informing me that their lost horses were branded with a half circle over an X, I begged him to examine mine, which were branded with a hat over the letter A, and he left the room to do so. He had been gone some time, and I was losing all hope of his getting back in time to do me any good, for the boys were dragging me out of the saloon for the crowning act of the drama, when my countryman rushed up with the Sheriff, who convinced them, with some little trouble, of their mistake. It seems that I had been taken for a noted young horse-thief named Alf. Harris, to whom, unfortunately, I had a slight resemblance. In the usual devil-may-care way peculiar to the southwest, the self-made deputies in my case "went it blind." At last I was set at liberty with some off-hand apologies from the men who, five minutes before, were glorying in the thought of seeing my body dangling in mid-air at the end of a lariat. After making these scant apologies the gang insisted on my "setting up the drinks" because I looked so much like the "cussed little thief." They took it as a good joke, but I felt like the frog in the fable. I repaired to my stopping-place in town and got to bed somehow, but so overstrung were my nerves that it was three long weeks before I was able to think of making that homeward trip again; and for months afterwards I never passed that identical hitching spot, even in broad daylight, without a nervous trembling, like ague, taking possession of me. I need hardly add that I never forgot any of my commissions again.

E. LANGLEY JONES.

UPRISING IN ALABAMA.
UPRISING IN ALABAMA.
Negroes Attack a Sheriff's Posse, and State Troops Called Out.
MONTGOMERY (Ala). May 4th — Tela.
State Troops Called Out.

Montgomery (Ala.), May 4th.—Telegrams report a bad condition of affairs in Lowndes county, growing out of the recent lynching of a negro murderer by a white mob. The negroes have been threatening vengeance, it seems, and to-day the Sheriff, with posse, went to Sandy Ridge and arrested fifteen negroes. On the way back to Hayneville, the county seat, the posse encountered a mob of armed negroes. A conflict ensued, and two of the white men were wounded and several negroes killed. After several volleys the negroes dispersed. They are reported to be assembling again in large numbers, and the Sheriff has telegraphed to the Governor for troops. Four companies from Montgomery are now leaving for the scene.
emerson-shepard-hayneville-1888-05-03.A5:
MOB VIOLENCE.

Lowndes County, Ala., Disturbed.

The Governor is Asked to Send Troops Immediately.
He Consents and the Second Regiment Leaves For the Scene.
The Trouble Caused by the Lynching of a Negro Murderer.
Reports Are Meagar and Conflicting, But it is Said a Clash Occurred in Which a Number of Whites and Blacks Are Killed.
Special Dispatch to The Appeal.
Montgomery, Ala., May 4.—This evening, at 5 o'clock, Gov. Seay received a telegram, signed by the citizens of Sandy Ridge and Fort Deposit, alleging that there was danger of mob violence in Lowndes county and asking for troops. The Governor replied, addressing them in the term of signature, and directing attention to section 4,703, of the code of Alabama. At 6 o'clock the Governor received a call from the sheriff of Lowndes county for troops by telegraph, stating that it was necessary to repress mob violence.

The Governor immediately ordered to the point of trouble, which is supposed to be Sandy Ridge, in Lowndes county, Col. Thomas G. Jones, of the Second Alabama regiment, with the Montgomery Grays and Blues and Mounted Rifles on a special train. They left at 11 o'clock p.m. for Letohatochee, and will probably reach Sandy Ridge, which is about eight miles in the interior, by daylight.

Another account received by telegraph from Fort Deposit states that the grand jury, now in session in Lowndes county, found indictments against about thirteen negroes, who were to be arrested by a posse of sheriffs. A number of the negroes showed fight and were reinforced by an additional mob of armed darkies, when a general fight ensued after they were summoned to surrender. Several whites were slightly wounded. A number of the negroes are reported killed and wounded. The rest were dispersed by the whites and a number carried to jail in Hayneville, the county seat of Lowndes county.

Many other conflicting accounts are circulating tonight, but the telegraph accounts are so meagre and conflicting, full and reliable news cannot be given with any degree of accuracy until tomorrow. The troubles in Lowndes county since Theo. Calloway, colored, shot and killed, near Sandy Ridge, Mr. Gresbam, an inoffensive white citizen, about a month ago, and who was subsequently lynched by hanging him in Hayneville, were thought to be over. But the renewal of the feud today marks another era in the bloody chapter which it is believed has its origin from the above mentioned lynching.

The negroes in Lowndes outnumber the whites fully ten to one and unless the State troops that went to the scene of trouble restore law and order, further bloodshed is apprehended. Sandy Ridge is about twenty-five miles from here and cannot be reached except by mounted messengers.
emerson-shepard-hayneville-1888-05-03.A14:
BLOODSHED AVERTED.
The Lowndes County Negroes Overwhelmed by the Troops.
The Lowndes County Negroes Overwhelmed by the Troops.

MONTGOMERY, Ala., May 4.—The troops returned from the scene of the trouble in Lowndes county at 4 o'clock this afternoon. They left everything quiet. They assisted the sheriff in arresting a number of negroes for whom warrants were out. There was great fear of trouble and every indication of it from the fight of Friday, in which two deputy sheriffs were shot. The presence of the troops had a good effect all around, and after being on the grounds some hours and marching fifteen miles they were withdrawn at the request of Col. Jones, the commander of the troops and the sheriff of the county.

PEACE NOW PROBABLE

It is thought that the trouble is all over, and that everything will be in the usual peaceful attitude. The deputies who were shot are doing well, and one of them was on duty to-day. It is not known that any negroes were hurt during the trouble. There would have been no difficulty but for resistance on the part of some negroes to the arrest of some of their number for whom warrants had been issued, and for their threats to resort to dreadful extremities.
emerson-shepard-hayneville-1888-05-03.A17:
DYING IN THE SWAMPS.
The Lowndes County Rioters Paying for Their Lawlessness.
The Lowndes County Rioters Paying for Their Lawlessness.

MONTGOMERY, ALA., May 6.—Two negroes who were in the fight at Sandy Ridge, Lowndes county, on Friday, are reported to be fatally wounded, no hopes being entertained of their recovery. The wounded men were taken to the swamps by their friends, and only one of them has been seen by any white man. Their names are Kit Webb and "Shack" Means. Bob Meriwether is reported to be in the swamps wounded. The five ringleaders gave themselves up to-day, saying their followers have gone back on them since the visit of the military Friday and Saturday. None of the negroes are dead.
emerson-shepard-hayneville-1888-05-03.A19:
A PLOT TO MURDER THE WHITES.
Discovery of an Alleged Extensive Conspiracy Among Alabama Negroes.
St. Louis, May 9.—Several reliable gentlemen
Discovery of an Alleged Extensive Conspiracy Among Alabama Negroes.

St. Louis, May 9.—Several reliable gentlemen reported at Montgomery, Ala., the following particulars as to the purpose and extent of the plot laid by the negroes at Sandy Ridge, Lowndes County. A negro who was mortally wounded made some very startling revelations. He states that Friday night last was the time appointed to massacre the whites. Meetings were held by the lodges to raise money to purchase ammunition to kill the whites if they attempted to arrest the negroes. The principal negro engaged in the plot was Bob Robinson, who was president of the meeting. Bob spoke very bitterly against the whites and implored his brothers to rise up in arms against them. Neal Mangum was also deeply implicated in the darling plot and was secretary and treasurer of the lodge. They claim to have lodge societies throughout the United States who have resolved to avenge their fallen ones and protect their color in the future at all hazards.

The negro claims that Lowndes, Crenshaw, and Butler counties have the largest clubs and fully competent to do their duty. They state that they have endured the mistreatment of the whites long enough and propose to put an end to it or there will be bloodshed. All the members of the lodge were notified by the leaders that if they failed to be present at the meeting Friday to do their duty in the proposed massacre of the whites, they would be put to death.

The above statement is from Emerson Shepherd, under oath, in the presence of four witnesses. This negro was fatally shot in the fight with the sheriff's posse last Thursday evening and has since died.

Forty-eight of the negroes engaged in the riot have been jailed. The sheriff's posse and the state troops seem to have put an end to the trouble for the present, but another outbreak is liable to come sooner or later.
emerson-shepard-hayneville-1888-05-03.A25:
A SOUTHERN SENSATION. Another of those Alleged Massacres that Never Come to Pass.
MONTGOMERY, Ala., May 9.—Emerson Shepard, a negro who was fatally shot in the fight with the sheriff's posse last Thursday, before dying revealed an alleged plot of the leaders in the Lowndes county riot. He states that Friday last was the time appointed to massacre the whites. Meetings were held by the lodges to raise money to purchase ammunition with which to kill the whites if they attempted to arrest negroes. The principal negro engaged in the plot was Bob Robinson, president of the meeting. Neil Mangum, secretary and treasurer of a lodge, is also deeply implicated. They claim to have large societies throughout the United States who have resolved to avenge their fallen ones and protect their color in future at all hazards. The negro claims that Lowndes, Crenshaw and Butler counties have the largest clubs and are fully competent to do their duty. They state that they have endured the mistreatment of the whites long enough, and it is proposed to put an end to it or there will be bloodshed. All members of the lodge were notified by the leaders that if they failed to be present at the meeting Friday and do their duty in the proposed massacre of the whites they would be put to death. Forty-eight of the negroes engaged in the riot have been arrested and jailed. The sheriff's posse and State troops seem to have put an end to the trouble for the present, but another outbreak is liable to come sooner or later.
emerson-shepard-hayneville-1888-05-03.A26:
THE USUAL TREATMENT.
Down in Alabama the vicious colored man has again turned himself loose, and the troops have been called out to suppress him. It seems that several colored men, in one section of the State, have recently been taken out and hung be the neck until dead. At least they were left hanging for from two to twenty hours, and when takan down manifested no active interest in present mundane matters.

Of course, some of the colored men who were not hung, objected to this sort of treatment, and had the courage to meet in assembly and say so.

Just as soon as this was done the noble Caucassian, whose bravery of course none could question, met at the place where turpentine whisky could be had easiest, and at once the cry was raised that the colored men meant to take care of themselves, and this being so, the Governor of Alabama must send troops to that section at once. In their haste they overlooked the statutory provisions governing such cases of legal slaughter, and appealed direct to the Governor instead of asking the Sheriff to do so.

Heretofore, it seems, that the killing necessary in every four years could be attended to direct from state headquarters, and thus save some time.

But this time they had actually to pay for a second message, by way of the Sheriff, and then the machine moved off finely.

The next we hear of it is this:
"A report from Sandy Ridge says a posse of whites and about 150 armed negres came in conflict this afternoon. Several white men were slightly wounded; some negroes are reported killed and wounded. The negroes were temporarily dispersed."

The Associated Press is controlled wholly in the interest of the making assassination respectable, and no one will ever know from that source anything else but blame for the colored men.

The Des Moines News tells in a brief item one of the common features of life for the black man in Alabama when it says: "Every crime committed in the South is at once laid at the door of some poor black man, and whether innocent or guilty, he goes on the chain gang or to the gallows as the victim of rabid race prejudice. All that the white ravisher of a woman has to do in order to escape justice is to help raise a mob to hang a negro for the outrage that he himself will have to answer for in the courts of heaven. Smarting under such injustice, the Alabama colored men would be poor wretches indeed if they showed no spirit of resistance."

Some day there will be a better and more just spirit animate the white people of Alabama toward the colored men before the law. But when?-the Lord only knows, and He seems to have moved out of that State!

Ottawa, May 4. May 4. Sir William Ritchie, Chief-Justice of Supreme Court of Canada, came down to the Senate this afternoon, endowed with the power of Deputy Governor-General, and assented to several bills passed this session. Among them was the act to ratify fisheries treaty, which thus becomes a statute of the Dominion.

Oil Struck at Lagrange, Ky.

LAGRANGE, Ky., May 4.—At 7 o'clock last night a good flow of natural gas was struck near this place, and for a time the flame was uncontrollable. The gas was found at a depth of 150 feet, and in a hard strata of limestone.

Dr. Bliss Critically Ill.

WASHINGTON, May 4.—Dr. D. W. Bliss, of this city, who was physician-in-chief to President Garfield from the time he was shot by Guiteau until his death, is seriously ill of heart affection, and his recovery is doubtful.

Cust of Garibaldi.

WASHINGTON, May 4.—A life-size bust of Garibaldi, made in Italy, and presented to the Senate by the Garibaldi Monument Association, of Washington, has been placed in a hall of the upper lobby of the Senate.

Threatened Catholic Revolt.

LONDON, May 4.—The people of a number of parishes in Ireland have warned the priests that if the Pope's rescript against the League is read in the chapels they will protest against it by leaving.
emerson-shepard-hayneville-1888-05-03.A35:
NUBS OF NEWS.
A party of log drivers in Baraga county, Mich., attempted to thaw some dynamite over a cook stove in their shanty. The result was a terrific explosion which killed three men.

Philadelphia had two hangings on Tuesday. One of the persons executed was David Vincent, who killed a sailor, and the other was Robert G. Hall, an actor, who killed Lillian Rivers (his mistress), the wife of James W. Rivers, last June.

The governor of Alabama asked the sheriff of Lowndes county for an account of a recent lynching of a negro, and the sheriff replied practically that his excellency might mind his own business. The sheriff and his posse then had a fight with a party of negroes, and the former sent to the governor for troops.

A package of $41,000 in national bank bills was sent last Saturday by express from New York to Washington for delivery at the treasury department. Upon being opened the package was found to contain only blank brown paper. It is believed the money was stolen before the package left New York, and not in transit.

St. Paul's cathedral at Buffalo, N. Y., was almost entirely destroyed by fire yesterday morning, owing to an explosion of natural gas. At least a dozen other explosions occurred at different points throughout the city. Four firemen were badly hurt in Pierce's Hotel by an explosion which occurred while they were putting out a fire.

W. C. Chamberlain, of Texas, has returned from Paris, where he went to be treated for a wolf bite by Pasteur, perfectly well. Another man bitten by the same wolf has since died of hydrophobia. Mr. Chamberlain felt the first symptoms of the disease before arriving in Paris. Pasteur feared it was too late, but the treatment proved efficacious.

The firm of Nicholson, Frost & Co., dealers in glassware at Boston, who recently failed, have discovered that they have been robbed of at least $10,000 by their bookkeeper. The peculations, which were not confined to the ledger accounts, have extended over several years. The firm has also lost several thousand dollars by dishonest salesmen.

A Sensation at Fayetteville.
Special News-Obc. ver.

FAYETTEVILLE, N. C., Aug. 22.—Saturday two negroes were lodged in jail here charged with an assault on a young white lady Monday night. The jailer discovered three squads of negroes around the jail armed with guns, pistols, dirks, &c. He sent for help and the few citizens on the streets at that hour, 1:30 o'clock, and the police went to his assistance. The negroes fled but three were captured and lodged in the prison from which they hoped to release the prisoners. Wednesday the town was excited. The negroes made deadly threats. That brave body of soldiers, the Fayetteville Independent Company, was held in readiness for any outbreak.

This morning at 2 o'clock watchers discovered bands of armed negroes at the jail. The soldiers made a swoop and captured several more. They are now on trial before four magistrates. No grave fears are felt as to further trouble at present. The excitement not being so great. It appears that the negroes were led by Tom Broadfoot, an ex-radical office holder, intelligent, and leader of his race. This makes the white men solid for Democracy. The color of a man proclaims his politics, and every white citizen of the State would be the same if he could know of the malignancy of the Radicals, and that means negroes in this city.

WHITE MEN, READ.
"WHITHER ARE WE DRIFTING?"
Something for Thoughtful, Self-respecting White Men to Reflect Upon.
[Fayetteville Observer.]

The town of Fayetteville has been the scene of tumultous and wild disorder for the past few days, which came very near ending in bloodshed and a war of races.

Two negroes had been committed to jail for an assault with a deadly weapon upon a white woman. The difficulty occurred in Rockfish township; a trial was had, the accused failing to give bond, they were committed and sent to jail in Fayetteville last Sunday.

Monday night following, the jail and surrounding premises were occupied by a mob of negroes armed with guns and pistols, led by a colored man, Tom Broadfoot, who himself was armed, and who had sent word to the negroes to meet him there with arms. The cause of all this, or rather the pretext, for there was no cause, was said to have been a wild rumor that the negroes were to be taken out of jail and lynched! No such threat had been made and no officer of the county or town had any such apprehension. The jailer and family were aroused about two o'clock in the night and sent to the chief of the night police for assistance. Numbers of our white people were aroused and sent over to the jail where, with magistrate D. Jones, who seeing that trouble and bloodshed was imminent, dispersed the turbulent negroes after disarming them.

Tuesday night the same scenes were re-enacted, but Sheriff Fisher, who had prepared for "any emergency," had the Fayetteville Independent Light Infantry armed and equipped, ready and within easy reach, whose presence only was necessary to show to the riotous negroes that they meant business, and that business was to preserve peace and order, and maintain the supremacy of the civil law.

Only a few weeks ago a terrible riot among the negroes occurred on these streets; the officers were assaulted, and a yelling, hooting crowd of infuriated and unreasonable blacks threatened to rescue two prisoners from the custody of the City Marshal, whose coolness, courage and discretion then prevented a bloody riot. This same City Marshal on last Tuesday night had two guns presented at him by negroes. Much praise is due to the cool-headed judgment and courageous conduct of Sheriff Henry C. Fisher and City Marshal Flowers, and the other officers who by the well executed plans, prevented the shedding of blood, which seemed imminent, during the week and before.

The Independent Company, its officers and men also deserve the thanks of the people of the county and State, as the protectors of our people, the defenders of law and the conservators of peace.
Now we are led to ask—whither are we drifting?
White men of Cumberland county and of North Carolina, what is in store for us, with the condition of things as here indicated, to be followed by the dire consequences of negro supremacy!
Farmers' alliances, knights of labor, prohibition, all sink into utter insignificance, when we are here confronted with the fact that the negroes intend to enforce the color line and precipitate the race issue. The negroes stand up in solid column and threaten the overthrow of all law and order, and become a law of their own making, subservient only to their own unreasonable and untamed will.
We do not propose to threaten any one, and while we deprecate all manner of riot and disorder, yet we warn the negroes and their leaders, that the law must and shall be enforced, if the whole power of the county and State is necessary to be used in its enforcement.
We are informed that certain leaders among the colored race here use violent, intemperate and incendiary lauage of late towards the whites as a race. The recent work is but the natural outcome of such languages. We warn them to desist, before the evil consequences of such language is visited upon their own heads. "Curses will come home" to them who utter them, and if any blood is unfortunately spilt, these incendiary leaders will be held responsible, and the whites will see to it, that the law is upheld, be the consequences what they may.

The offenders have been tried; their purpose being here shown to be to precipitate a collision between the races. They have failed, and will have to answer at the next Superior Court. Shall it stop now? We shall see!

THE TROUBLE IN FAYETTEVILLE.
A few weeks ago the local press excited its readers by flaming head-lines: "Negro Riot," "Rescuing Prisoners," and the like. The military company in Fayetteville was called out and a few colored men were arrested and tried on the charge of "unlawful assembling," or atttempting to rescue prisoners from jail.

We have made careful inquiry in the matter and the facts are about as follows: Two colored boys in the country were arrested on a charge of assaulting a white girl; lynching was freely talked of; the colored people were alarmed and put out sentinels to watch the jail at night and give the alarm in case there was any effort to take the boys out. The jailor discovered the sentinels, became alarmed himself and had the parties dispersed. On the second night the military company was called out and every colored man found in the neighborhood of the jail was arrested and the country was thrown into a great fever of excitement over the report of a terrible riot and imminent danger of bloodshed in Fayetteville. These men were tried on charges above stated and bound over to superior court.

There was no unlawful assembling. The colored men simply feared these boys would be taken from the jail and foully murdered. They quietly put sentinels there to watch and notify the public in case of an effort at foul play, or to take such steps they might think best calculated to protect the prisoners. If the colored men had any reason whatever to fear these boys would be lynched, they had a right to take any lawful steps to save them from such cowardly murder. The colored people of Fayetteville have not forgotten the foul murder of Archie Warden on the very steps of the court room in which he was tried and in the
fayetteville-fayetteville-1888-09.A6:
hands of the high sheriff of the county. They do not want to see another such blot fall upon the fair name of Cumberland. They read in the press the frequent occurrences of such crimes throughout this Southland. These are an intelligent an honest, an honorable, a brave people. They are not law-breakers, and the men arrested are among the quietest and most intelligent.

We take occasion now to warn the colored people of Fayetteville and all other places against violence, hasty judgment and indiscreet or unlawful action. At the same time we believe the colored men of Fayetteville thought in this case as many others think, that the time has come for this lynching to be stopped. Many of our white citizens think so and with the proper manly actions on the part of white men and colored men who oppose it, it can and will be stopped. We do not believe in violating one part of a law to execute or preserve another part, but we would like to see all parts of the law observed as far as possible, and when the preserving of innocent life is simply preserving and executing the law, to give blood and life is a common duty incumbent upon all rational beings and one disregarded by no race except the American Negro.

The American Negro has many faults brought upon him by the great cause, slavery. Twenty-three years should have freed him from many of his faults.

The colored people here were misinformed as to the charge against these boys. The charge was a common assault while it was thought to be indecent and criminal. There was really no danger of the boys being hurt and there was really no danger of the colored men interfering with anything, but as this is a political year, all advantage is taken of colored men's mistakes. It is said a drunken white man first started the rumor of probable lynching. The whole affair is very unfortunate. It was published by the papers that Broadfoot James Tucker and English Gee were put in jail. Neither of these gentlemen were in jail, but gave bail the first night of the trial. They did as any honorable men would have done and no wrong can be proven against them.

A TAX WAR. Indian Territory Cattlemen Keep Off the Collector and His Posse By Force of Arms. St. Louis, May 24.—Advices from the Indian Territory say that serious trouble is existing in Pickens county, Chickasaw Nation, between the non-residents and the Chickasaw officials on account of the collecting of the $1 per head tax on all stock. The stockmen have organized, armed themselves with Winchester rifles, and for the past few days have kept back the Collector and his posse by force of arms. Collector McLish has appealed to Gov. Guay, at Tishomingo, for help to enforce the collection of the tax and put down the mob. The militia has been called out by the Governor, and is unable to cope with the mob. The United States Government will be called upon for help by the Indian authorities. There are great fears entertained of a general warfare between the non-citizens and Indian authorities. The former are largely in the ascendency, and well organized for a stubborn resistance. Suicide Or Murder.
Suicide Or Murder.

St. Louis, May 23.—At 4:15 this afternoon, a second-story room of No. 310 Chestnut street, was forced open by the police and two brothers, John F. and Charles G. Fuhrmann, were found dead, having apparently ended their lives together with poison. They carried on a little jewelry shop and sub-let the rooms of several buildings on Chestnut street. They had lived here for thirty years, and were thrifty, industrious men. When last seen, Monday evening, they were in excellent health and good mood. The idea of suicide held by many is not satisfactory to the police, as there are no signs of poison and no known cause for the deed. Fuller investigation of the affair shows conclusively that death occurred from natural causes. The brothers were very old, one being eighty and the other seventy-four years. The younger was in very feeble health, and the elder subject to apoplexy.

The Trunk Murderer's Trial.

The Trunk Murderer's Trial.

St. Louis, May 22.—The Missouri Supreme Court yesterday received the mandate of the United States Supreme Court in the case of Hugh M. Brooks, alias Maxwell, the Englishman convicted of the sensational Southern Hotel murder. Court adjourned without fixing the date for the execution. It will not convene again until June 4, when the date for the execution will be named and the mandate forwarded to the shoiff. Maxwell was much affected when he was informed that the State court would, in a few days, dispose of his case forever. His trans-Atlantic friends are working hard on Secretary Bayard. Minister Phelps, Minister West and Governor Morehouse. A half dozen different petitions are in circulation in this city, but the signatures are few.

A Lover's Crime.

Richmond, Ind., May 23.—(Special.)—Lulu Penny, daughter of a prosperous farmer, who had been teaching school at East Germantown, had a frightful experience there last night with Frank Shank, a worthless fellow, who had been a suitor for a long time, and had been discarded. He cut her throat, and in the attempt to kill her indicted another ugly cut in her cheek. Her physicians pronounced her injuries fatal last night; but were sanguine of recovery today. Shank is in jail, and says he was drunk, and supposes he did it when she was upbraiding him.

A Murderous Preacher. St. Louis, May 28.—A singular story of a Baptist preacher killing his father-in-law,

comes up from Indian Territory. Parson Cantrell is a Seventh-day Adventist, and his father-in-law, Deacon Coffey, went to his field near Jintown, last Sunday, where Cantrell was plowing, and not only remonstrated against his working on the Lord's day, but undertook to kick him out of the field. The parson resisted and split his father-in-law's head open with a hoe.

A TRAIL OF BLOOD.

A Murderer and Two Robbers Break Jail At Monticello, Ind., After Murdering the Sheriff.

Delphi, Ind., May 25.—Three prisoners in the Monticello, Indiana, jail—Ed. Chamberlain, Albert Benson and Robert Catterson—assaulted Sheriff Joseph Henderson and escaped last night. The Sheriff went into the corridor to lock the prisoners in cells, when Chamberlain struck him down with an iron bar, and all three rushed to the jail-office window and jumped. The Sheriff's injuries are fatal.

Chamberlain is under indictment for murdering Ettie Wittenberg, his sweetheart, at Reynolds six weeks ago. Benson and Catterson were tramps awaiting trial for highway robbery. Both have served time in Michigan City penitentiary. Before leaving all three wrote long letters. Chamberlain said that the unwholesome atmosphere of the jail was undermining his health; that this was his only chance for his life; that he had done right in murdering his sweetheart and would advise others in similar situations to do the same thing. The tramps said that there was no chance for them to get justice in Indiana.

The whole country for miles around is aroused, and it is not thought that Chamberlain can possibly escape.

The Sheriff entered the jail with a cocked revolver, but was completely trapped. His wife witnessed the affair and gave the alarm.

Viroqua, Wis., May 25.—Information was received here to-day of the murder of four persons last night in the town of Kickapoo. Mr. and Mrs. Reuben Drake, an old couple, were shot dead in their own house by unknown parties and the throats of their two little grand-children were cut from ear to ear. The lifeless bodies were found this morning, when neighbors made an investigation because of the unusual quiet about the house. The old couple lay on the floor and the children were stretched in their beds. Everything was turned upside down inside the house and it is supposed that the murder was the result of an attempt at robbery.

The old man had been known to receive pension money, and it is supposed that the robbers were in quest of this. As Mr. and Mrs. Drake were fully dressed, it is supposed the murder occurred early in the evening. The neighborhood is greatly excited, but there is no clew to the perpetrators.

It is not known how much booty was secured from the house. The officers who inspected the premises found that the house had been thoroughly ransacked, drawers overturned on the floors, and everything left in great disorder. The murderers probably demanded Mr. Drake's money and upon his refusing to disclose its hiding place, if indeed he had any in the house, shot him and then his wife. The children were no doubt awakened by the noise and for fear that they might identify them, the murderers apparently decided that they too must be sacrificed, and cut the throats of the innocent witnesses of the terrible deed to make their own escape more certain.

Mr. and Mrs. Drake had been residents of this county for forty years. They lived a quiet and secluded life.

New Orleans, May 22.—A special from Greenville, Miss., says: "Three horrible and unjustifiable crimes were to-day avenged by the nanging of one white man named Grahame and two men named David Moore."

New Orleans, May 22.—A special from Greenville, Miss., says: "Three horrible and unjustifiable crimes were to-day avenged by the nanging of one white man named Graham, and two negroes named David Moore and Willard Hall. The execution took place in the jail yard at Bolivar, the county seat of Bolivar county. About two thousand people witnessed the hanging. David Moore, a large negro, had killed one of his companions during a game of dice. Willard hall, a big six footer, while drunk, killed a fifteen-year-old boy. Graham, the white man, was about twenty-five years old and of rather a delicate appearance. He was hanged for killing two white men on Sunflower river.

Cut a Young Girl's Throat. CAMBRIDGE CITY, May 23.—[Special.]— Frank Shank cut three gashes in the throat of Lulu Penny last night while the latter was on her way home in company with Frank Winter. Winter had jumped over the fence for a moment, leaving the girl in the road, when Shank seized her and slashed her with the knife, then turned and walked away. Sensational Damage Suit. Special to the Indianapolis Journal. MARTINSVILLE, May 29.—The case of Wm. L. Hickey, of Elnora, Daviess county, Indiana, vs. J. C. Kiefer, wife and daughter Carrie, of this city, was begun in the Circuit Court here to-day. Mr. Hickey married a daughter of Mr. Kiefer, about two years ago; about six months ago Mr. Hickey's wife left him, and returned to her parents, and has lived with them since. Mr. Hickey sues for $20,000 damage, claiming that his wife's affection for him was alienated by the defendants. About seventy witnesses are to be examined on behalf of each side. Adams & Newby are attorneys for the plaintiff, and Harrison & Renner represent the defendants. A Summons from Judge Lynch.
RICHMOND, May 29.—Sheriff Bond to-day found the following in his mail, referring to the worthless fellow who so murderously assaulted his former afflianced, Lulu Penny:

EAST GERMANTOWN, May 28.

Sheriff of Wayne County:

Dear Sir—We desire and forcibly obligate you as sheriff to deliver to Judge Lynch one Frank Shank, on May 29, at 12 o'clock midnight, to 100 armed men, masked at the door. Tell no one to deny in danger of life. The girl is going to die. Signed,

COMMITTEE.

Policy Shops in Trouble.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

EVANSVILLE, May 29.—The squabble with the policy shops in this city, which were shut down a few days ago by the discovery of a fraud on the part of the players, culminated today by the filing of forty different affidavits against the dealers by one of the holders of a winning ticket. The natural result of this will close up every shop in the city, unless the "joints" put up their losses, which aggregate over $10,000.

A $10,000 Damage Suit.

MARION, May 29.—Cynthia J. Fisher entered suit to-day against James Shaw, demanding $10,000 damages. The suit is based on the accidental killing, two years ago, of plaintiff's husband by the defendant. While repairing a flood-gate, the maul which Shaw was wielding slipped from his hands, striking Fisher's head, and inflicting fatal injuries.

Thieves Arrested.

Thieves Arrested. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

MARION, May 29.—On Saturday night Henry and Lee Casey stole a wagon-load of groceries from Bailey & Brownlee. They were hotly pursued, and escaped only by stealing a horse on which they took flight. Last night the Caseys, who are desperate characters, were arrested at their home, eight miles south of this city, and were lodged in jail.

Minor Notes.

While drilling in a lime kiln, north of Delphi, yesterday, a premature explosion of dynamite occurred and three persons were injured. Alex. Smith was terribly injured, and it is thought will die.

Mrs. Nancy Mace, an aged lady residing at Nabb Station, fell out of a wagon while riding along the highway and received serious injuries. She has since suffered partial paralysis and is now lying in a critical condition.

At a citizens' meeting in Lafayette, under the auspices of the Merchants' and Manufacturers' Exchange, it was decided to form a gas trust for the importation of gas into that city. The gas will probably be brought from Kokomo, at an estimated cost of $260,000.

James Blair, a wealthy and prominent farmer of Jackson county, in attempting to secure a swarming colony of bees that had settled on the limb of a tree, twenty feet from the ground,

sawed the limb between himself and the body of the tree. His fall to the ground resulted in fatal injuries.

ILLINOIS.

McClaughrey Has Not Yet Been Pardoned, and Such an Event Is Not Likely to Occur.

SPRINGFIELD, May 29.—No pardon has yet been granted boodler McClaughrey, the announcements to the contrary notwithstanding, and the prospects are that none will be within the next few weeks, at least. A delegation of his friends waited upon the Governor to-day, but received no intimation of what would be done, and were afraid to press the matter fearing it might result to the disadvantage of the boodler.

Brief Mention.

Mrs. H. H. Wally, of Blue Mound, divided her money between her husband and her son, laid out her wedding clothes in her room, and then cut her throat from ear to ear.

William S. Phillips has been appointed superintendent of the State Blind Asylum at Jacksonville. He is a son of the recent incumbent, the Rev. F. W. Phillips. The appointment gives general satisfaction.

A farmer named Roberts, living near Springfield, was fleeced out of $600 by confidence men last week. They got the money from the old fellow last week and told him they would return it to him when they came back to buy his farm.

Miss Andrew J. White, of Peoria, drowned herself in a neighbor's cistern on Monday. She was about fifty-two years of age, and belongs to a highly-respected family. She had been insane for some time, and had been home only about two weeks from Jacksonville.

Dr. A. C. Ferre, of Aurora, a prominent dentist, was found dead in bed on Monday night. He committed suicide by swallowing morphine, and left a letter saying he was tired of life. Dr. Ferre was an active G. A. R. man, member of the A. O. U. W., Masons, and Mutual Aid Association.

EMMA PREWITT,

Of Kentucky, the Youngest Novelist in the Country.

It is said of nearly all authors who have attained distinction that they have exhibited predilections for literature at an early age, but it is seldom that their productions are submitted to the criti-

cism of the world until they have reached eighteen or twenty years of age. Miss Prewitt perhaps stands alone, in this country at least, as having ventured upon the literary sea at the age of fourteen. Emma Prewitt was born in Madisonville, Ky., on April 9, 1873. Her father was Dr. J. H. Prewitt, a dentist of some renown in Western Kentucky. The life of the young author has been uneventful, having been spent within the quiet precincts of her native town, with the occasional diversion of a trip to the East in company with her father. It was his desire to give her a thorough musical education, and she was sent to Louisville and Washington for the advantages of study in that art afforded by those places. But it was soon manifest that her choice was literature, and at the age of twelve she made contributions to the local papers which were very acceptable, both in composition and wonderful imaginary faculty. During the next year she made many contributions to the Kentucky papers and published a few magazine articles. It was at this time, too, that she began work upon her first novel, "Karlene Hoy," which has just been accepted and will soon be issued by the Lippincotts.

Miss Prewitt lost her father by death last December. He was a prominent member, vice president, of the American and Southern Dental Associations, and these bodies have taken great interest in his daughter, to whom she is known as the "Daughter of the Association." She is an honorary member of them both.

Henry Starkey, a widely known citizen of Detroit, is dead.

Natural gas has been struck in abundant quantities in the Sequatchie Valley, twenty-two miles west of Chattanooga, Tenn.

Miss Tilla Coleman was burned to death at Birmingham, Ala., a few days since. While lighting a fire with kerosene her clothing ignited and she rushed from the house wrapped in flames and rolled down a flight of stairs into the midst of a group of women, setting fire to half a dozen of them. The house was burned down.

County Judge J. Tartar, of Somerset, Ky., was drowned in Pitman creek a few evenings since while attempting to cross it in his buggy. The stream was swollen by heavy rains. Congressman Frank Finley was in the buggy with him at the time, but jumped out and swam ashore. He made an effort to save his friend, but was unsuccessful. The horse and buggy were recovered. Judge Tartar leaves a widow and seven children.

Mrs. Jane Duke died at Hartford, Ky., a few days since in the ninety-seventh year of her age. She enjoyed the distinction of being the first white child born in Ohio County, a territory which at the time of her birth included more than one-third of Western Kentucky. She was in many respects a remarkable woman, and maintained her activity in a great degree, and her eyesight and memory up to the time of her death.

Harry Smart was sentenced in Louisville, Ky., a few days since, to imprisonment for life for killing Meisner Green and Belle Ward four months ago.

The jail at Greensburg, La., was burned a few nights ago. There was only one prisoner in the building, a young negro charged with horse-stealing; he was cremated.

I. S. Albritton, a "picked" juror in an Atlanta (Ga.) murder trial, has been sentenced to jail for twenty days and to pay a fine of $200.

At North Birmingham, Ala., a few nights ago, Henry Brown, colored, shot and killed D. Johnson, white. The shooting was the result of a quarrel about some trivial matter. Brown escaped.

The report of the keeper of the Georgia penitentiary shows that during the last two years the proportion of female convicts in Georgia has increased more than twenty per cent.

Hon. John P. Campbell, an able lawyer and ex-member of Congress, died suddenly at his home in Hopkinsville, Ky., recently, in the sixty-ninth year of his age. He was at one time a member of the Missouri Legislature.

John Corbitt died recently at Nashville, Tenn., from the effects of an overdose of laudanum, taken with suicidal intent. The cause of the deed is not known, but it is supposed that he was suffering from mental aberration.

Andrew Johnson, a cripple, living near Red Hill, Ky., while digging in the ground, recently, unearthed a copper kettle filled with gold and silver coins. The kettle was inscribed "October, 1788." The treasure amounted to over $2,000.

Fire at Lynchburg, Va., a few days ago, destroyed Moorman's tobacco warehouse; the Dental chewing-gum factory; Hefernan's sash, blind and door establishment, and Ainslie & Bro's carriage works, causing a loss of over $50,000; insurance; $21,000.

Governor Seay of Alabama has removed the civil and political disabilities of John R. Taukersley, of Crenshaw County, convicted of murder in 1878, and sentenced to the penitentiary for ten years. Joe Williams, Hardy Pope, Hardy Lewis and Jack Bailey escaped from the jail at Kingston, Tenn., a few days ago. When the sheriff and jailer opened the door the quartet pounced on them and after securing the sheriff's pistol made a break for liberty. After a lively chase, in which a large number of citizens joined, the jail birds were all recaptured.

At Fayetteville, Tenn., a few nights ago, Yerb McElroy, about eighteen years old, clerking in L. Garneau's bakery, became involved in a quarrel with ex-Policeman W. H. McCown, about the way some oysters were served. McElroy stabbed McCown in the throat, cutting an artery. McCown bled profusely, blood running from his eyes, ears and nose. Jesse Brundage, a twelve-year-old son of Mr. H. Brundage, of Leon, Ala., was accidentally killed a few days ago, at the steam gin of John Merrill. Later he denied all knowledge of the crime. Harrison said he had been drinking heavily.

WATERLOO, Ia., Nov. 29.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—John Bowman, the wealthy Marshalltown ex-brewer, who was recently enjoined by the district court from selling liquor in the original package and fined $1,000, was yesterday committed to jail for contempt of court in disobeying Judge Stevens' injunction. Mail Agents Reinstated.

WATERLOO, Ia., Nov. 29.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—A number of mail agents on the through runs across the state who were discharged for offensive partisanship just before the election, have been set at work again, the postoffice department having learned that the new men were unable to handle the business satisfactorily. Captain E. G. Miller, of this city, who was dismissed from the Cedar Rapids and Council Bluffs run about a week before the election, began work again Tuesday, and he says that nearly all the old men are back on the through runs. They have not been reinstated, but simply set at work again, where they will remain until the new administration is ushered in and they can be reappointed.

The Great Calf Case.

WATERLOO, Ia., Nov. 29.—The defendants in the case of Robert Johnson vs E. V. Miller, better known as the "Jones County Calf Case," have perfected an appeal to the supreme court from the decision of the September term of the district court in this city. This will be the fifth time that this case has been to the supreme court, and if a new trial is granted it will be the seventh trial of the case since 1877, when the case was begun. The calves were originally worth $45, but they have already cost the parties to the litigation about $20,000, and no one knows when the end will be reached.
