WATERLOO, Ia., Nov. 29.—The Union Mill

Iowa Mills Reduce Their Output.
WATERLOO, Ia., Nov. 29.—The Union Mill company of this city, who own the largest flouring mills in the state, have decided to reduce their output of flour about one-half for the present and close up several of their elevators in different parts of the state. The cause of this action is a falling off in the demand for flour throughout the state. The managers say that they are but following the course of the Minneapolis and other large mills, and they expect to be able to start up all their mills again soon after the 1st of January.

A NOVEL CASE.

General Sickles Has a New Method of Life Insurance.

New York, Nov. 20.—General Daniel F.

Life Insurance.
NEW YORK, Nov. 29.—General Daniel E. Sickles was defendant in a law suit yesterday that brought to light a novel transaction. Six years ago he made an agreement with Mrs. Frank F. Cave to insure her husband's life in various companies. He was to pay all the expenses, and in the event of Cave's death was to receive two-thirds of the insurance money. Cave's life was then insured in various companies in sums aggregating $4,000. Cave died in 1886. General Sickles had some trouble collecting some of the policies, but finally succeeded in getting $39,991, after having paid out $4,320 in premiums and assessments. In all he paid $10,766 to Mrs. Cave, charging her with one-third of the expenses. The widow then concluded she wanted all the money collected under the policies on her husband's life, and sued General Sickles for $27,991, the amount he retained. The jury decided that General Sickles must pay the widow $2,500 more, but he is still $20,000 ahead on the transaction.

MEMPHIS, Tenn., Nov. 29.—News is just received of a lynching in Crittenden county, Arkansas. Jim Smith, a negro, met the wife of a white farmer in the road and made an insulting proposal to her. She fled and he pursued and was about to overtake her, when the approach of a horseman frightened him away. The woman reported what had occurred and Smith was arrested by a deputy sheriff. On the way to jail at Marion the two were met by a mob of white men who took charge of the prisoner and filled him full of bullets.

A Broken Bow special to the Omaha Bee says: Last night Sheriff Penn brought Haunstine and wife to Ansley, where the murderer was left in charge of the deputy. The wife and her father came to Broken Bow. An excited crowd followed the woman and her father as far as the hotel. Later Haunstine was brought to town in a carriage, and waiving examination, he was held for trial, and was secreted by the sheriff.

The wife was examined before Judge Leese, and plead not guilty to the charge of being an accessory after the fact, to the murder of Roten and Ashley. Taking the stand, she testified that on the day of the murder she was getting dinner, when Roten and Ashley drove up and fastened their horses to Haunstine's wagon and then came into the house. Haunstine and wife invited them to take dinner, which they declined. Haunstine gave to one of the men the clock, afterwards found in the dead man's pocket. Then the visitors went out, and Haunstine and wife sat down to dinner. After eating, Haunstine arose and went out, closing the door, and his wife washed the dishes. She heard two shots, but did not look out, as her husband often practiced about the place. After fifteen or thirty minutes he came in, saying: "I've done a bad deed," and "we must get out of here." Witness did not see the bodies, but was told that they were under the pile of hay. He wished her to stay there, but she would not with two dead men lying around. Taking bedding and a few things, and a roll of butter, the couple started, with their horses hitched to the buggy of the deceased, and leading the horses of the dead. As they started Haunstine looked at a watch he had taken from one body, and it was 3 o'clock. That was the first witness knew of the robbery of the dead. Haunstine left the lead horses at a vacant stable and drove to Arnold. They met a number of teams on the road. At Arnold they changed horses and drove down the Loup, traveling all night and all the next day. They avoided towns and slept near haystacks. Near Madison Haunstine hired out to husk corn and worked several days. At Madison he sold the team and buggy for $75 and sent the wife to Columbus by train. He came on another train, as witness says, "thinking maybe 'twould be cheaper going separate."

Haunstine's wild looks and foolish conduct are hardly those of a sane man. The feeling in Roten valley and vicinity is terribly bitter and threats of lynching are frequent. But the better feeling will no doubt prevail and the prisoner be given a fair trial.

Chief Arthur, of the Brotherhood of Engineers, left Chicago for Cleveland, but before leaving disclaimed any knowledge of the action of the St. Paul men, and said that as the men acted as individuals they would not receive a dollar of assistance from the Brotherhood, and not a dollar of Brotherhood money would be applied to assist the switchmen now on strike.

PLAIN talk was the order of the day at the session of the International Council of Women in Washington on the 30th ult. In a quarrel on the 30th ult. near Effingham, Ill., Henry Lane, a farmer, killed his wife and then committed suicide.

WORKMEN, in remodeling an old house at Piqua, O., found on the 30th ult. the bones of four children, and the discovery revived a tradition that they were the heirs to a considerable fortune, and disappeared many years ago.

DURING the seven days ended on the 30th ult. there were 179 business failures in the United States, against 212 the previous seven days. In a quarrel on the 30th ult. over a nickel at Atlanta, Ga., Noil Stark shot dead his brother, Flaentz Stark.

BENJAMIN E. HOPKINS, assistant cashier of the Fidelity Bank of Cincinnati, was sentenced to eight years in the penitentiary on the 31st ult.

A FIRE on the 31st ult. in the editorial rooms of the New York Tribune did considerable damage.

The strike in the State printing office in Lansing, Mch., resulted on the 31st in the places of the strikers being filled by nonunion printers.

Sullivan has cleared $25,000 in England.

Alexander Beaton's wife and grandchild were burned to death at Boulandree, N. S., on Monday night.
The father of Brook, alias Maxwell, the murderer of Preller, is coming to try and save his son's life.
Jem Smith's manager says his man is willing to fight Sullivan for $5,000 a side, but not for some months to come.
G. O. W. Griffen has been appointed Health Inspector at Truckee, and a building has been secured for a pesthouse, if needed.
There is a report in Truckee that John Regli, son-in-law of Elle Ellen, died in the German Hospital at San Francisco yesterday.
"Coffee Jack's" dance house, a seamen's resort at San Pedro, was burned yesterday. This incident may have an effect on the sailors' strike.
Mrs. Cline, a Carson woman, who had for some years been a magnetic physician, committed suicide on Wednesday by taking chloroform.

MARIPOSA, July 19th.—Last January a young Mexican named Julian Medon was found hanging to a tree on Moore's Hill, eleven miles south of Mariposa. It was plainly a case of lynching. Suspicion was directed to several cattlemen, and the officers were censured for their lack of activity. It appears now that they have been quietly at work, and through detectives trailed up the guilty parties. Just what evidence was secured has not transpired, but some sort of clue was obtained.

Last week Jim Westfall and Jack McGuire were arrested, and to-day a third party, named Smithers, was bagged. All three are in jail. Rumors are circulating that indicate more recruits for the same institution. Evidently some of the gang have "squealed."

A TRAGEDY IN IDAHO.
Lew Durfee Shot and Killed by E. J. Wright.
AN ATTEMPT TO LYNCH WRIGHT
He is Struck in the Neck by a Bullet From the Mob-Wright is Dying.
A horrible tragedy was enacted at Pocatello, Idaho, yesterday afternoon, which resulted in the death of one man and the fatal wounding, by a mob, of another. The first word of the affair to reach this city was in the following dispatch to THE HERALD:

Pocatello, Idaho, December 22.—[Special to THE HERALD.] J. Wright shot and instantly killed Lew Durfee, a passenger brakeman this afternoon about 2.30. Wright immediately surrendered; intense excitement; lynching feared; prisoner escaped about 5.30; pursued; fired at frequently; brought down by a shot in the neck; the officers brought the prisoner to the depot building, keeping the mob at bay with cocked revolvers. The prisoner is said to be dying; depot surrendered by a mob.

FULL PARTICULARS

came later in the following dispatch:

Pocatello, Idaho, December 22—[Special to THE HERADD]—A fatal shooting affray occurred in this place about 2.30 p.m. L. F. Durfee, a passenger brakeman, on the Oregon Short Line, got into a row at the Pacific Hotel with Constable Neilson, between whom there was an old grudge. Neilson was badly beaten and finally called upon E. J. Wright, commonly known as "Buck," for assistance. Wright also got the worst of the row and pulled his gun but was prevented from using it. Shortly after Wright and Durfee met in Dr. Bean's drug store and Wright again pulled his revolver, and without a word, shot Durfee twice in the face, killing him instantly. Wright then surrendered to the officers, but afterwards escaped. He was pursued and shot at frequently, finally receiving a bullet in the neck which brought him down. He was brought to the depot and the building is now surrounded by a howling mob of switchmen and brakemen intent on lynching him. The officers are now holding the mob at bay with drawn revolvers. Sheriff Taylor is en route from Blackfoot with a posse for the protection of Wright, but it is feared he will not arrive in time. A later dispatch says that Wright is fatally shot and is now dying.

The Pocatello Murder Case.
A fatal shooting scrape occurred at Pocatello last Saturday in which L. F. Durfee, a passenger brakeman on the Oregon Short Line, came to his death from gunshot wounds inflicted by E. J. Wright, a citizen of that town. At the coroner's inquest Mr. Wright was exonerated from all blame for the killing but as he is to have a preliminary hearing before a proper officer we withhold an extended notice and all comments until his case is disposed of. Mr. Wright is now in jail at Blackfoot suffering from the gunshot wounds he received during the day of the trouble and is improving slowly for one so dangerously wounded. As soon as he recovers sufficiently he will have a hearing for the shooting. The remains of the party killed were brought to Blackfoot Monday attended by a delegation of friends and after funeral services in the M. E. church conducted by Rev. Mr. Stull they were buried in the Odd Fellows' Cemetery. During the afternoon of Saturday last excitement ran high at Pocatello and Sheriff Taylor were buried Taylor who was at the time at Camas, had to engage an extra train to take him to the scene in order to preserve peace and prevent further bloodshed.

FOREIGNERS FIGHT.

WILKINSON, Pa., April 3.—A terrible riot took place in the Polish-Hungarian quarters of the town Sunday night. The foreigners celebrated Easter by drinking immense quantities of beer and whisky. Towards night they got to fighting among themselves and a big riot ensued. Stones, clubs and pistols were used in the melee. Women and children took part, and at midnight nearly one hundred persons lay on the battle-field, all more or less injured. The police were summoned but were not strong enough in numbers and were routed by the rioters. Officer Nolan was probably fatally injured in the scuffle. He was struck on the head with a stone and his skull fractured. The whole police force was called to the scene, and, after a hard struggle, succeeded in subduing the rioters and arresting about forty of them. The battle between the Poles and Hungarians lasted from seven in the evening until eight o'clock next morning. Five persons were taken to the hospital with their heads crushed and bullet holes in their bodies. Four of the number will certainly die. Their names are Stanibars, Vnoyenchi, S. Schwerts, Krockie and Michael Ellorish. The brewer who furnished the rioters with two wagon loads of beer is to be arrested. More than fifty of the Poles and Hungarians were picked up out of the roadways yesterday morning and taken to their respective homes. The scene where the rioting took place resembled a battle-field, all covered with blood.

TRIPLE MURDER.

LIMA, O., April 3.—Last evening Patrick Hughes, Dave Gallagher and James Stockey were stabbed to death in a fight with Dave Crowder and William Goins, colored. Crowder and Goins were passing Manning's saloon on Main street, when a quarrel ensued. Hughes' heart was cut in two with a razor. The most intense excitement was caused by the murder and the police were unable to keep the streets clear. A mob formed and the various police stations and the county jail were visited, but the murderers were not found. It was learned late at night that the authorities had arrested them soon after the murder and had them in hiding, fearing mob violence.

MURDER IN WAR TIMES.

St. Louis, April 3.—The sheriff of Callaway County arrived here last night with Robert Clawton, who killed three men in this State in October, 1862. Clawton and his brother were living on a farm near the little town of Portland, in Callaway County. The brothers had been troubled by incursions made by bushwackers, whose visits were credited by him to the malice of a neighbor named Lein Coates, and the two killed Coates. Jerome and Dick Maddox ran out into the street towards the Clawtons, who turned and killed both. Robert Clawton fled the country and has not been heard of until recently, when he was arrested in Wood County, Texas, on the charge of killing a man named Frazier. He admits the triple killing, but claims it was done in self defense.

ITALIANS OBJECT.

New Castle, Pa., April 3.—At the limestone quarries at Carbon, the employes, who are mainly Italians, were notified a week ago of a reduction in wages. The sheriff in response to a telegram from John A. Logan, Jr., son of the late Senator Logan, who is superintendent of the quarries, sent a posse to the scene this morning in anticipation of trouble. A conflict occurred this afternoon in which several shots were exchanged, and a man named Angelo Nocero received a bullet wound in the knee. About one hundred Italians are engaged in the strike.

ZEPH DAVIS TO BE HANGED.

Chicago, April 3.—The jury in the Zeph Davis trial returned a verdict of guilty of murder as charged, and decided that he should suffer the penalty of death. Davis is the young negro who killed little Maggi Gaughan in the boot heel factory of Greene Bros. in this city about a month ago because, as he said, "she sassed him." The murder was one of the most atrocious ever known in this city.

BORED A HOLE.

TEXARKANA, Ark., April 3.—Saturday night eight of the eighteen prisoners confined in the Miller County jail with an auger bored a hole in the wall and made good their escape. Bloodhounds are on the trail. Jim Doles, a negro, and forger of school warrants, and a man giving the name of Dave Dixon, for burglary, are among the number who escaped.

SLASHED TO DEATH.
Two Men Killed at Lima, O. in Race-War.
Prisons Scarched by a Mob Bent on Lynch ing the Murderers-The Authors lies Hide the Killers.
LIMA, O., April 2.—At nine o'clock tonight a crowd of colored men, Wm. Goins, Dave Crowder, Sam Thomas and Wm. Harrison attacked Tim Casey and James Clark in front of Manning Brothers' saloon. During the afternoon there were several fights between the colored men and the Irish boys. A bitter feeling has existed between the two races for years. On election day this spirit is more manifest than at any other time, and to-day was no exception. Goins and Tim Casey engaged in a fight in front of the Dela Flora saloon about seven o'clock, but they were acquainted before any serious damage was done. Later in the evening Goins, with a number of other colored fellows, started out in search of the Casey crowd and were awarded with finding them in front of Manning's. Without a word they went at it. After fighting with stones and clubs a few minutes the colored man drew knives and commenced shashing right and left. E.L. Stokey and Jim Clark, with several others, were standing away from the crowd, the fight had drawn, when Goins and his followers started for the outside, cutting their way through. Hughes was cut in the back, the knife penetrating the heart. He staggered into the saloon and fell just inside of the door dead. Gallagher received two wounds—both inflicted from behind. One cut was just below the heart, and will prove fatal. The other one was a little below the upper one, and penetrated the left lung. Stokey was badly, but not seriously injured. He was stabbed from behind and the blade of the knife striking one of his ribs alone prevented it from penetrating his heart. He was also stabbed in the hip. The murderers fed. The news of the murders spread like wildfire, and in a few minutes Main's feet was a mass of surging humanity for several squares. The excitement was intense, and as the report that some of the murderers had been arrested gained currency, a mob started for the police station on High street. Arriving there, to the disappointment of the mob it was found that the objects of their search were not there. It was proposed that the county jail be visited, and the mob, fully two thousand strong, started on a run for that institution. Arriving there they were met at the door by Sheriff M. P. Hoagland. They demanded the keys, which the sheriff refused, and said the murderers were not there. The mob insisted, and surrounding the building threatened violence if they were not admitted. After parleying it was decided by the sheriff to admit three of the ringleaders and let them visit the cells and report. This was done, and the men not found. The committee reported, but the mob was not satisfied, and breaking in the doors rushed for the entrance to the jail proper. Sheeriff Hoagland had just recovered from a sick spell, and seeing that further resistance was useless handed the keys to Lew Hunter, who happened to be with the sheriff at the time of the attack. The mob thinking that this was a move to hide the keys, jumpet on Hunter and gave him a terrible beating and took the keys away from him. One of the mob made an attempt to brain Hoagland with a heavy piece of iron, and was only prevented by the surging of the mass. While this was going on within the jail an excited crowd of several thousand persons filled the jail yard and the street in front for many squares, and no attempt was made to present the hanging of the murderers should they be found within, the unanimous sentiment being that they should die. After securing the keys the mob opened the big iron doors, and, after opening every cell in the jail, gave up the search in disgust.

THE USUAL END OF A FEUD.
A very distressing triple murder occurred in Logan county, this State, last week. The trouble originated from a feud which has existed for several years. The parties to it are the McCoys and Hatnelds. Some years ago a quarrel took place between them, started by the Hatfields interfering in a private matter of the McCoys. As a result of this quarrel James Hatfield was killed. Three of his brothers lynched two of the McCoys for the murder, after subjecting them to most inhuman treatment. This was but the beginning of the warfare between these two families. They have been deadly enemies ever since. The enmity showed itself during the past six years in the poisoning of horses, wells, burning barns and other deeds of similar character. "On Wednesday night," says the party who brings the news, "the McCoy family, consisting of father, mother son and daughter, were at home quietly sleeping, when the odor of burning cloth awoke the daughter. She jumped up and running to the door found the house was on fire. Scarcely had she opened the door when she was snot dead. Her brother, nearing the noise, ran out, and before he had gone a dozen steps he two was snot and mortally wounded. The parents were sleeping in a part of the house not directly connected with the main building, and were not at first awakened. When they did awake the house was nearly all in a blaze, and they barely escaped with their lives. The mother ran out first. As she entered the yard the prostrate forms of her son and daughter—the one dead and the other dying—met her gaze. Scarcely had she uttered a sound when a bullet pierced her breast and she fell. Though not dead when last heard from, there was no hope of her recovery. The father managed to escape with his life. As he ran he fired in the bushes from which the last shot had come, and it is reported that one of the assailants was wounded. Then he fled, fearing to remain even to look after his property or family. It is suspected that the old enemies of the McCoys were the assailants."

HATFIELDS DECLARED INNOCENT.
An Interesting Interview With Hon. John B. Floyd.
HISTORY OF THE WHOLE CASE.
CHARLESTON, W. VA., January 16. State Senator John B. Floyd, of Logan county, was interviewed to-day in regard to the McCoy-Hattfield vendetta that has been raging between members of rival gangs living in Logan county, W. Va., and Pike county, Ky. Mr. Floyd lives within a few miles of the Hatfield settlement and is intimately acquainted with the history of the difficulty from its origin up to the present time.

In response to your correspondent's inquiries, Mr. Floyd said:

"Yes, I saw that report in the Register and Intelligence about the killing of James Vance and some of the Hatfields over in Logan county. I also saw the report of the killing of some of the McCoys and the burning of McCoy's house on the first of January published in the Enquirer, which was charged to the Hatfields.

"Both of these accounts make the Hatfields appear to be outlaws and murderers. Now since you have mentioned this I want to tell you that I have known all of the Hatfields for fifteen or twenty years, and lived within eighteen miles of them the greater part of that time, and I never regarded them in the light of criminals or desperados, and they are not so regarded by the people of Logan county. On the contrary some of these Hatfields are regarded as being of the very best and law-abuting citizens of that county, and they are.

"The history of the trouble which has brought about the present state of affairs in Logan county, W. Va., and Pike county, Ky., began during the war of secession. However, when the war ceased the differences between the Hatfields and McCoys seemed also to have practically come to an end. But in 1882 Ellison Hatfield went from his home in West Virginia across Tug river into Kentucky, only a few miles from his home, to an election over there. During that day three of the McCoys deliberately laid their plans.

TO ASSASSINATE HATFIELD,
and they carried them out by cutting and shooting him to pieces. Before the McCoys could get out of reach they were themselves killed by some of the relations of Hatfield. This having taken place in Kentucky the Hatfields and a great many other citizens of Logan county were indicted in Pike county, Ky., for the killing of the McCoys. This was in 1882, the same year of the killing. After the indictments were made no further steps were taken in the matter by the Kentucky authorities, and the matter rested for five years. This was because the authorities of Pike county evidently regarded the McCoys as the aggressors; and they knew that the McCoys were just about as bad as men get to be. Every one thought the trouble was over with. But a few months ago a man by the name of P. A. Cline, who is a lawyer, and who is also, I am told, the jailor of Pike county, concluded that he would stir up the thing again and make some money out of it, knowing that the Hatfields owned some good property in Logan county, W. Va. So Cline got copies of the old indictments to which I referred awhile ago, and went over to Frankfort, Ky., about three months ago, and made, God and the Governor of Kentucky only know what kind of representation as to the desperate character of the Hatfields, and succeeded in getting the Governor to offer a reward of $2,700 for the Hatfields and grant a requisition for them. This done he let the Hatfields know of the fact by some of his co-workers.

IN THE CAUSE OF BOODLE, and at the same time intimated that if he could get some four or five thousand dollars he would have the proceedings put to an end. Well, he agreed to take $225, and the money was placed in the hands of A. J. Auxier, a prominent lawyer of Pike C. H., for Cline, according to his agreement, and Cline made a pretense of trying to have the reward and requisition recalled, but in the meantime his co-workers, Jo n kite and Frank Phillips, have been making efforts to get hold of the Hatfields and secure the reward. They got old Randal McCoy in with them and that gang with their followers have been bullying everybody along the border for the last two or three months. The Hatfields kept out of the way so as to avoid trouble. The result of this muranding was the burning of McCoy's house and the killing of his son and daughter on the 1st of January, and an effort to kill Old Randal McCoy himself. Everybody knew that McCoy had been waylaying the houses of the Hatfields, trying to kill them, and when this occurrence took place it was at once placed to the credit of the Hatfields by these men who were after them to better enable them to capture the Hatfields. The circumstances surrounding the Hatfields may have been sufficient to justify them to try and kill McCoy, but they did not, and knew nothing of the burning of McCoy's house and the killing of his son and daughter, as can and has been shown beyond all question.

"But this is not the end of this terrible history. It runs down to more recent date and the tragedies connected with it are more shocking than anything that has occurred in our State in recent years; and it shows beyond all question that the pursuers of the Hatfields are desperate characters who have no regard for life or property. Let me read from this letter just received by me from a lawyer and good citizen of Logan county:

THE M'COY-HATFIELD FEUD.
Another Bloody Chapter in the History of Extermination.
[By telegraph to the Dispatch.]
NEW YORK, January 19 — A. Ch

New York, January 19.—A Charleston (W. Va.) special says: Information reaches here from Oceana, Wyoming county, that another bloody chapter in the McCoy-Hatfield feud was enacted Saturday night last, in which the lives of five McCoys were sacrificed. It will be recalled that about the beginning of the new year the feud, which had been stilled for some months, broke out again between the two families, in which the Hatfields were worsted. After the funeral of the victims the Hatfields proceeded to annihilate the family of Randall McCoy. They surrounded his house across the Kentucky line, set fire to it, and drove McCoy's wife, son, and daughter like sheep into the shambles to be ruthlessly slaughtered. Randall McCoy escaped to the woods. This was followed by the McCoy raid in West Virginia recently described, in which three of the Hatfield party were killed in a battle in the woods.

All the details that have yet been received of Saturday night's massacre are simply that the Hatfield gang made a raid on the house of Sim McCoy, brother of Randall. The McCoys were completely surprised. Mrs. McCoy was tied to a tree and shot to death. The eldest son was next tied up and riddled with bullets. Sim McCoy barricaded the back room and made a weak defence of his home against great odds. Finally the Hatfields set fire to the house and McCoy and his two youngest children were burned to death.
mccoy-son-1888-01-18.A15:
The Outlaws.
Late information in regard to the trouble between the Hatfields and McCoys seem to indicate that the latter are the real aggressors. While the Hatfields, or some of their friends may have burned Randall McCoy's house and killed several members of his family, the McCoys had been spying around and watching the homes of Hatfields for months to kill them.

The gang that is now hunting down the Hatfields is made up of men of equal lawless and desperate character, and are on a mission of vengeance and speculation. So far they have killed James Vance, an old man a relative of the Hatfields, it is said without provocation, robbed his house and carried back to Kentucky what money they could find.

As an evidence of the brutality, ferocity and ruffianism of the posse it is said, and no doubt true, that after they killed Vance they crowed and shook hands over his body, and Randall McCoy sent word to Capt. Hatfield that he intended to kill him, cut out a piece of his flesh, broil and eat it. If the Hatfields have committed crime against the law, they should be punished by the law, but such bloodhounds as these put law to shame.—Wayne News.

CHARLESTON, W. Va., Feb. 1.—Col. W. E. Mahan, the agent sent out by Governor Wilton, of this state, to ascertain the status of the now famous Hatfield-McCoy war, has returned to this city, and yesterday afternoon presented his report to the governor. He says he found all the Hatfields to be law abiding citizens, who have the respect and confidence of every one in the neighborhood, and that, while many depredations have been committed, peace has been restored and the belligerent parties on both sides have disbanded.

The Hatfields and McCoys are related, and the recent outbreaks seem to have been caused by persons in Pike county, Ky., resurrecting indictments against the Hatfields which were found against them five years ago. These persons went to Frankfort, Ky., and had rewards offered for the Hatfields, and then came into West Virginia, under guise of officers of the law, and kidnapped Thomas Chambers, Andrew Varney, Selkirk McCoy, D. D. McCoy, Moses Christian, Samuel, D. D. and Pliant Mahon and Valentine Hatfield into Kentucky and placed them in Pike county jail, where they are still confined.

Your correspondent was given a letter which Senator Floyd received from a prominent and well known attorney of Logan, and from which the following was taken:

"On the 6th of the month thirty men came from Kentucky, with Frank Phillips and John Kite at the head, took charge of Anderson Hatfield's family, drove the women and children before them down the river to the mouth of Grapevine Creek, where they took L. P. Smith and other members of his family and Capt. Hatfield's wife and children, and drove them like beasts before them some four or five miles down the river to William Ferrell's. There they made Ferrell and another man go with them as guides, and started for where old man John Vance lived, telling the women and children all the time that they would leave them at Ferrell's, and if one of them told of their being in the country they would kill them as they returned to Pike. Then, with the guide above referred to, they proceeded up Thaker's creek to Vance's, where they found old mar James Vance, and, pursuant to a threat made some time before that, old Randal McCoy fired on him, and that was followed by shots until the body of the old man was torn to shreds, and, as I understand, with no earthly provocation. All that they could say, I suppose, was that he was a relative of and a friend of the Hatfields. From there they came to the head of Island creek, and we can't tell what they will do next. The reward of Governor Buckner has put on the trail of the Hatfields a set of lawless men, who not only have no respect for man, but, brute-like, destroy women and children. The whole country is alarmed, and every one feels that there is no security to life or property. We are listening all the time to hear of other horrible deeds."

It is said that Randal McCoy threatened to kill Capt. Hatfield, cut a slice from his body and roast and eat it. The region where this trouble was carried on is wild and mountainous, and it would be almost impossible for troops to do any good in the part of the country where the Hatfields and McCoys travel. The troops ordered to the frontier have been ordered back, and as matters now stand soldiers will not be needed to quell the desperadoes.
mccoy-son-1888-01-18.A17:
After a good many more murders, the state of Kentucky concluding that if she did not interfere there might be bloodshed, offered heavy rewards for Ans Hatfield and several of that gang. Frank Phillips, a McCoy, was then deputy sheriff of Pike county, Ky. Taking the warrants, he led a gang into Logan county and captured the stepfather of a man for whom he had a warrant. Soon after another raid was made into Logan county, W. Va., resulting in the capture of more prisoners. Then the Logan county "regulators" gave notice that if there was any more "fooling" somebody might get hurt. This kept the peace for a while, but not long. On New Year's night about a dozen Hatfields surrounded Randall McCoy's log cabin and called on him to come out and surrender. McCoy was naturally timid about obliging them, whereupon they set the house afire. All the occupants of the house except one, including an old woman and a young girl, were shot down. The escaped man was Randall McCoy, whose wife, four sons and a daughter have been killed.

Capt. Vance, of the Hatfields, was the next to fall. The McCoys went to his house when he was away and robbed it. An old woman, Mrs. Vance, Capt. Vance and Capt. Hatfield, were returning home, when they met the McCoys. Capt. Vance ran down the mountain side he was descending at the time. As soon as the McCoys saw him they opened fire, which the captain returned. Mrs. Vance was about half way between the two. She held her ground, the bullets flying by her thick and fast. The McCoys yelled to her to sit down, but she wouldn't. They called out that they would shoot her, and she told them to shoot. Presently she heard Vance shout: "Rally on the top of the hill, boys." Then she knew he was hit and delirious. The old lady told them they needn't fire any more. It is supposed that this murder was not inspired by the noble purpose of the former ones, but that it was simply to acquire possession of the captain's rifle.
And it is supposed that the fight will go on yet many years, or until some one in authority with nerve puts a stop to it.
But the violent death of the last Hatfield and the last McCoy may occur in the meantime.

Assaulted a White Woman.
Special to the Gazette.

FORNEY, Tex, Oct. 24 — At about 4 o'clock this evening a negro tramp assanlited a white woman, the wife of the section boss, named Henry Boyd. He passed the section house and seeing her alone he drew a pistol on her and scared her into submission. He made his escape on the evening train, but it is now reported that he was arrested on the train between Descott and Dallas.

THE PARTICULARS.
THE PARTICULARS. Special to the Gazette.
Special to the Gazette.

FORNEY, TEX, Oct. 25 — The negro who committed the rape on the wife of the section boss, about four miles east of here, yesterday afternoon was arrested on the train between Mesquite and Dallas. A pistol was found on his person and the officer carried him to jail in Dallas. This morning Constable P. E Yates of this place, with the proper papers, took the early train and brought him back to Forney, arriving at 10 o'clock. The negro was placed in a room with several others and the lady was told to pick him out. She did so immediately and the negro said he was the man, but if they would let him go he would never do so again. Immediately a great racket was raised by the crowd, and they demanded his release, and cries of "Hang him!" "Shoot him!" "Burn him!" filled the air. After the crowd had become quiet, the officers started with him to jail at Kaufman. They had got about a mile on the road, when on crossing a small creek a body of armed and masked men overpowered them and took the negro and hanged him to a bois d'arc standing near, and then shot him in several places. After the news came to town that he had been hung, 'Squire I. S. Moore went out to the place and held an inquest on the remains. The verdict of the jury was that the deceased had come to his death at the hands of some unknown persons. His remains were brought back to town and left exposed to view for perhaps an hour or more before he was taken away. The colored people would not let his body be buried in their grave yard, and your correspondent was unable to learn exactly where he was buried. The town is all quiet now, but for a few hours this evening the excitement ran very high. This is one of the quickest punishments ever visited on a criminal in this county during the past dozen years. The crime was committed on yesterday at about 4:30, and he was hung to-day at 1:10 o'clock. The negro's name was Sam Smith, and his residence was in Dallas.

STATE NEWS.
Officers are elected for the Eagle Pass Trigation company.

The cotton crop this year at Kilgore will be the shortest ever known.

The drouth in Crockett is at last broken, and fine rains have fallen.

There is much friction in the management of the lunatic asylum at Austin.

Medina county's harvest home will be one of rejoicing this year. Pastures are in fine condition and so are cattle.

The Brazos river syndicate is still buying up lands at Columbia, contiguous to the future great city, but the bar remains unmolested.

There are now five more days of the Texas state fair and Dallas exposition, and people from the uttermost parts of the state are flocking in.

It is proposed to have some sort of celebration on the 15th of next month at Eagle Pass, when ground will be broken for the new irrigation ditch.

On a farm, 15 miles west of Sherman, James Rogers, a 12-year-old boy, was dangerously shot while shelling corn in a barn, by an unknown person.

An attempt was made two nights ago near Arnold to wreck an accommodation train on the Texas Pacific, which came very near being successful. No clue to the perpetrators.

The governor has telegraphed to Mr. Grady and the distinguished Georgians at the Dallas fair, extending them a cordial invitation to visit the state capital.

The colored rapist, Sam Smith, of Forney, is lynched, while the officers were on their way with him to Kaufman jail. The colored people of the place would not let his body be buried in their graveyard.

The little town of Castroville is now excited over the sudden and mysterious disappearance of Justin Haus. It is feared he was drowned while fording the Medina. He was the father of a large family, whom he leaves with little support.

State Health Officer Rutherford, on being asked what would be the effect of the cold spell on the quarantine regulations of the state, replied that the tendency was all right, but that there had not yet been enough cold to warrant any relaxation of the stringency of quarantine protection.

A brutal assault and rape was committed by a negro named Sam Smith upon Mrs. Henry Boyd, wife of the section boss, two miles east of Forney. He made for Forney and took the train, but was arrested between Mesquite and Dallas.

The fence cutters of Sulphur Springs are not satisfied with their work. Mr. Wagoner, who owns a pasture north west of town, has received the following notice through post: "Hopkins County, Tex.—W. B. Wagoner; Spool your wire. We are cutting. We are here first. Do as we direct. (Here is drawn a picture of a coffin). Dogs ain't worth a d—m. CUTTING BOYS."

MONTANA.
MONTANA.

An Indian Scare Among Settlers Near Flathead Lake.

HELENA March 27th A few days ago
An Indian Scare Among Settlers Near Flathead Lake.

HELENA, March 27th.—A few days ago word was received that the settlers north of Flathead lake had discovered the murderers of the three white men, committed last summer by Kootenai Indians, and had armed themselves to go in search of and punish the murderers. It would seem that they had accomplished their purpose, for a letter containing the following extract was received from a resident of that section Saturday.

"Here we are, all up at G. M. Lakins on account of the Kootenai scare. All of the families from Elliott's down, except Henry Bartlett's are here. Those above Elliott's, on this side, have gone to the Sheldon school-house. Those on the east side have retired to Ashley.

"The trouble arose from the lynching of two Indian murderers at Penny's mill. Though nothing definite has been learned it is understood that the Kootenais have taken the warpath.

"A squad of men from Selish are guarding the point of rocks. Another of our party are defending Lee's ferry and we are seeing to the Big Fork's ford. Don't be worried, for we don't anticipate serious trouble."

Nothing has been heard from that section since then, and it is presumed there has been no active hostilities.
slume-ashley-1888-03-31.A3:
THE MURDERS IN IDAHO.
How the Bloodthirsty Kootenias Killed Three Settlers.
SHELDON, Idaho, March 13.—[Correspondence of the Missoulian.]—One of the most horrible murders in the annals of pioneer life has just come to light having been committed last June. At present writing every man in the valley who has been informed is rallying to the call of outraged law and order. Before the sun is high in the heavens tomorrow the depraved Kootenai savages that perpetrated this shocking crime will have paid the penalty they so justly deserve, and an important step taken towards the settlement of the Indian question, which neither the military nor civil authorities have secured.

Three men unarmed and unsuspicious, were set upon by a half dozen savages as they sat at their noonday meal, murdered and robbed and their bodies consigned to the flames of their own camp to remove all evidence of the bloody deed.

The crime was the outgrowth of that wide liberty allowed the Kootenais, and the savage frenzy worked up at their medicine dances.

THE LOCALITY OF THE MURDER.

Wolf Prairie is about 50 miles from Ashley on the Libby creek tran, and has long been the scenes of medicine dances, only at last to supplant the mock tragedy of recital and pantomime by a shocking reality.

Although six in number the murder was done by the leader, who, lurking in a growth of small pine, deliberately waited till they all sat down on a fallen tree, and then fired, killing one and mortally wounding another at the first shot. Two more shots were required to finish the third man as he dashed wildly from the scene, and he joined his companions who had preceded him by a few seconds. The horrible stench from the burning bodies, together with the smoke, attracted another Indian, who was out hunting, he coming onto them in the midst of their disgusting work. They swore him to secrecy by all the oaths of a savage God. But the affair was first told around council fires by the actors themselves before the old man sworn to silence told it. There is scarcely a dissenting voice in the proposal to take the matter in hand and rid the earth of the most blood-thirsty wretches that a vicious and barbarous race can produce.
slume-ashley-1888-03-31.A8:
INDIANS LYNCHED.
And Trouble is Feared With Others of the Band.

ASHLEY, M. T., April 1 — On the 31st instant two Koctana Indians were arrested and placed in charge of the Deputy Sheriff. During the deputy's absence they were taken from his guard by a party of fifty citizens and lynched. They were charged with helping to murder three prospectors on Wolf creek last June. Trouble is feared with others of the same band, as the residents of the country are much excited.
slume-ashley-1888-03-31.A12:
HI YU SKOOKUM!

Authentic Account of the Flathead Murders, Indian Arrests and Lynching.

Two of the Three Kootenai Devils Swung From a Tree by Settlers.
THE FLATHEAD TRAGEDY.

A Straight Account of the Triple Murder and the Recent Indian Lynching.

From Mr. Charles V. Jones, who is just in from the Flathead lake country, is learned the first intelligible account concerning the recent lynching of Indians on Flathead river. The circumstances of their crime as detailed at their trial before Judge Lynch, by an Indian boy, were substantially as follows: Three Kootenais named Antley, Slume and Jonninna had been out hunting in the mountains, accompanied by three Indian boys. Coming down Wolf creek they ran across three prospectors and had dinner with them. Then they started on. After they had gone a few miles Slume suggested that they go back and kill the prospectors. Antley did not favor the proposition. Finally Slume told him he had a woman's heart—in other words that he was a coward. This Antley could not stand, so he consented to the killing.

"I'll show you that I have no woman's heart," he said.

When they got back to where the prospectors were Antley, to show he was no coward, insisted upon being permitted to do the killing himself. This being granted, he hid in the willows near by the prospectors' camp and awaited his opportunity. Finally he got all three of the men in line and fired. His bullet killed the first man, mortally wounded the second and crippled the third. The others now took part. The man who was mortally wounded was clubbed to death with a rifle, and the one who was crippled tried to get away and was shot down. It was a most atrocious murder.
Then the Indians started on their way again. After going two or three miles it was decided unsafe to leave the bodies as they had done, so they went back to burn them. Brush was cut and piled on the ground, the bodies were placed on this and the whole was set on fire. To show their delight in the fiendish deed, they gathered the green kinnikinnick and placed it upon the baking bodies to dry. Their theory was that it would be made fragrant with the burning blood of their victims. After the bodies were entirely consumed they continued on their way back to their own camp, boasting of the crime. A short time after the murder, a medicine dance was held on Tobacco Plains. At these dances the Indians get together, boast of their deeds of bravery, the number of men they have killed, and finally work themselves up into a perfect frenzy of rage against the whites. It was at this dance that the murderers told the rest of their crime committed on Wolf creek. The news reached the ears of the white settlers, and three week-ago to-day they organized for vengeance. About eighty men proceeded from Ramsdall's store to the Indian encampment some three or four miles away. It was very early in the morning, before the Indians were up. Slume and Jonninna were captured without difficulty. Antley was at another camp several miles up the creek, and before the whites could get there, he had been warned and made his escape. The two prisoners were taken over to Demarsville, where a deputy sheriff took them away from the party and handcuffed them together.

The boys, however, recaptured their men and took them across the Flathead river into the timber about a quarter of a mile. The oldest of the three Indian boys, who had been at the murder, was also taken along. Three interpreters were taken along in order that there should be no chance of injustice being done by an interpreter. The Indian boy told the story of the murder related above. Then Slume confessed in English his part of the crime and was exultant over it.

The verdict was death. The lynchers had but one rope and so hung the murderers one at a time. Jonninna was first strung up. He assissted them to fasten the rope around his neck. The other end was then thrown over a limb and he was pulled up. Slume was still handcuffed to him. Slume seemed to enjoy the performance hugely and laughed at his companion's struggles while strangling. Then
slume-ashley-1888-03-31.A15: A CORRESPONDENT of the Missoulian intimates that the settlers in some portions of the Flathead country are apprehensive of the Indians in that neighborhood. He says the settlers away from the thickly settled portion of the community have grave concerns as to their safety. So serious is the matter that on the 25th ult. a mass-meeting was held at Ashley and a committee chosen to draw up and circulate a petition to the Secretary of War asking that troops be sent to that valley "to aid the settlers in repelling any attempt on the part of the Indians to lay waste or retard" its development. The cause of the apprehended danger from this cause is a recent act of reprisal on the part of some settlers in hanging a couple of Kootenai Indians who had taken part in the murder of some prospectors last July. This they did in preference to turning them over "to the law and its uncertain results." The latter, however, would have been the most effectual way to avoid any sentiment of revenge on the part of the Indians towards the settlers.
slume-ashley-1888-03-31.A16:
Lynching Bad Indians.
Some weeks ago a warrant for the arrest of two Kootenai Indians was sworn out in the justice's court at Ashley, Montana. The Indians were arrested and placed in charge of a deputy sheriff. During the deputy's absence a party of citizens, numbering fifty or sixty, overpowered the guard, took the prisoners to the east side of the river, and, it is supposed, "made good Indians" of them. The crime charged against them was murder. It is alleged that these Indians assisted a third Kootenai in killing three prospectors on Wolf Creek last June. Two of these men were well along in years, and the third was a young man. After shooting them, it is claimed they were beaten over the head with six-shooters until life was extinct, and their bodies were then burned. It is asserted by responsible men that the above named "Mood Indians" confessed complicity in the fearful crime and made an open boast of their prowess. The booty received was $6 in money, a scanty supply of provisions and two ponies. The ponies, it is claimed, are now in the possession of the fugitive Indians. A company of fifty white men made a peaceful visit to Dayton Creek and had a talk with Chief Aenas, of the Kootenais, resulting, as claimed, in an agreement between the whites and Indians to bury the hatchet, Chief Aenas agreeing to turn over the fugitive Indian to the legal authority if caught. A correspondent writing from Thompson Falls gives the following account of the beginning of the trouble: "The first of July, 1887, Ben Thompkins, one Johnson and Daniel McDonald left Libby with two pack animals to prospect in the Kootenais. They never have been heard of since. There is considerable mail at Goodchild & Co.'s of this place for McDonald. Every one in this part is satisfied that they are the parties murdered."

slume-ashley-1888-03-31.A17:
HI YU SKOOKUM!
Two of the Three Kootenai Murderers
Hanged to a Tree.
A gentleman who came in from Flathead Lake Friday gave the Missoulian a vivid description of the recent stirring events in that section of Missoula county. Everything has assumed its usual quiet, and once more peace reigns supreme in Flathead valley.

The plans of the settlers to capture the three Kootenai Indians who murdered three prospectors on Wolf creek in June or July last were well laid out. Between forty-five and fifty of them gathered at Demersville early in the morning and proceeded in a body to the Indian lodges, located between one and two miles below town. The lodges were reached while the Indians were still sleeping soundly. One lodge after another was searched, and guards left to prevent an outtery or voice of warning, until the lodge where two of the murderers were sleeping was found. The names of these two Kootenais were John Ninna and Slume. They were forcibly taken by the settlers, who were all armed and determined to carry out their plans at all hazards.

The name of the third murderer was Antley. Antley was not there; he was in Smith's valley, several miles distant. As soon as the settlers left with their prisoners an Indian jumped upon the fleet st horse in the camp and dashed wildly away to Smith's valley. He went to warn Antley of the danger, and his mission was successful. The fugitive was notified and he fled in haste, probably toward the British possessions. It is stated that the settlers of Smith's valley had promised to arrest Antley, but they failed to do so, and he is probably forever safe from the reach of the vengeance of the people of Flathead Lake.

Ninna and Slume were taken to Demersville. A hasty consultation was had when the two murderers were hastened to the river bank, a skiff was procured, the savages were rowed across the river, never to return. The settlers acted cautiously, quietly, but determinedly. They resolved to hang the two Indians, instead of turning them over to the law and its uncertain results. The murderers were informed that they were going to be hung, and one of them defiantly retorted, "Hi yu Skookum," which means powerful good. It is said they made no attempt to conceal the murder of the prospectors, but even bragged of their savage instinct and of making the white man's flesh smoke and quiver in the flames.

They were taken into the woods lining the east bank of the Flathead river at that place, ropes were fastened about their necks and they were swung up to the limb of a tree. A short time afterwards the bodies were cut down and buried.

After this stirring event considerable excitement prevailed both among the whites and Indians. The latter packed up their duds and fled to the Arm of the Lake. Subsequently a report spread among the settlers of danger, when they organized a large company and, thoroughly armed, went down to interview the chief, Aeneas. When the Arm of the Lake was reached the Indians mixed in with the whites and acted in a defiant and warlike manner. Aeneas was on the road to the mission and a courier was sent after him with all haste. He was overtaken and induced to return, when a consultation was had, resulting in an amicable understanding. The settlers then returned to their homes, feeling much relief.

Nina, Slume and Antley were bad Indians, and the death of the two former occasioned little if any mourning. At latest accounts both the whites and Indians were entirely satisfied, and there is no danger of further trouble between them, so far as the muders are concerned.

The Indians gave an imperfect description of the three white men who were murdered on Wolf creek in June or July last. Two of them were elderly and the third was a young man. One of the men had gray whiskers and hair and his frame was spare. The other man was heavier and whiskers dark. The boy was medium size with light moustache. It is not unlikely that the three men reported missing by our Thompson correspondent last week were the same three who fell victims to the brutality of the Kootenais.

THE KOOTENAI TROUBLE.
Chief Eneas Admits the Justice of Hanging the Indian Murderers.

Arlee, Mont., April 22.—In his report to Maj. Gen. Ruger on the recent trouble between the Kootenai Indians and the settlers near Ashley, Agent Kenan says:

It is a fact that the citizens of that vicinity did execute two Kootenai Indians some time last month, and that a third one made his escape or he would have followed the fate of the other two. From diligent inquiries among the Indians of this reservation, I am afraid that the reported murder of three white men is true, and that no mistake was made by the citizens as to the identity of the Indian murderers. The white men were killed about the 17th of last June, at a place called Wolf creek, on the trail leading to Tobacco plains. The Indians who committed the crime, and who were lynched, are said to belong to the band of Chief Eneas, who have their homes on the reservation, and live about six miles north of the agency at Dayton creek. One of the murderers, who is still at large, confessed the crime to reliable Indians of this reserve. It seems that a party of some ten Kootenai Indians, while passing along the trail, noticed three white men encamped. One Indian proposed to two others to go to the camp and intimidate the whites. On hearing them the Indians fired over their heads, but the white men only laughed; whereupon the Indians decided to kill them. Two of the white party being seated eating in range, a bullet fired by an Indian passed through both men, killing them instantly. The third was fired upon and wounded, and was killed by the blows of an ax. No motive was given for the crime. I sent for Chief Eneas, of the reservation Kootenais, and he told me he had met a party of white men at Dayton creek. Their leader, one Kamsdale, told him they had hung two of his Indians, and were there to find out what he was going to do about it. It was explained to Eneas that a white traveller who had camped near Dayton creek, on hearing of the hanging of the Indians, mounted a horse and rode into Ashley and stated that the band of Eneas' were in arms; that they had attacked him, and he made his escape while the Indians were plundering his wagon. This was easily refuted by Eneas. The action of the white man who caused the excitement on the reservation is inexcusable. Chief Eneas, in his talk to me, stated that if murder had been committed by the Indians, it was nothing more than justice to hang the guilty ones, but was sorry that the lake settlers, took the law into their own hands and lynched the prisoners, as a trial, conviction and execution by due process of law would have a more salutary effect upon the Indians and prevent recourse to revenge. In regard to the state of things relative to the security of the white settlers. I cannot see what cause they can have for excitement, especially as the chief of the band to which the culprits belonged states that no trouble will come from him or his people, as it is a conceded fact that they were unjustifiable murderers of white people, and deserved their fate; whether by lynch law or otherwise. A move for the establishment of a military post in that region has a great tendency, I think, to stimulate some of the people to keep up excitement and to exaggerate the real state of affairs.

A Mob of Negroes Threatened to Lynch a Railroad Crew.
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., Oct. 10.—At Smith's mines, eight miles from this city, to-day, the crew of a freight train on the Birmingham Mineral Railroad narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of 200 negro miners. The train ran over and killed Clara Dickson, a negro woman, who was drunk and lying across the track. Her body was ground to fragments, and the train crew took a shovel and threw it into a ditch that ran along by the side of the road. This angered the negro miners, who had witnessed the accident, and they surrounded the train swearing that they would lynch every man in the crew. The negroes sent to a store near by for a rope, and then the train men all got aboard the engine, and before the mob suspected their intention they had cut loose from the train. The engineer pulled the throttle open and the engine dashed away, followed by a storm of bullets. The cab windows were broken by flying bullets, but none of the crew was hit. The negroes swear that they will kill any of this crew who attempt to run a train by there again.

NEGRO RIOT IN ALABAMA.
An Accidental Killing Causes a Riot at Smith's Mines.
BIRMINGHAM, ALA., Oct. 10—At Smith's Mines, eight miles from this city, to day at noon a freight train in charge of Engineer Brown and Conductor Brantly on the Birmingham Mineral Railroad ran over and instantly killed a negro woman named Clara Dickson, who was drunk and lying asleep on the track. Her body was ground to pieces and the fragments scattered over the the track for a hundred yards. As soon as the accident occurred 1,500 negroes collected around the remains of the dead woman and began to curse and make all kinds of threats to the train crew. When the train men attempted to remove the remains of the dead woman from the track the negro mob charged them. Stones were thrown at the train men and several shots fired. The negro mob then cried in one voice, "Let's lynch the murderers." Two negroes procured a rope and the mob rushed on the trainmen. The latter took to the engine and only saved their lives by cutting their engine loose from the train and escaping. The leaders among the negroes were drunken men. Great excitement prevails around Smith's mines over the matter.

Two Hundred of Them Try to Lynch Five White Men.
Two Hundred of Them Try to Lynch Five White Men.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., Oct. 11.—Two hundred negro miners at Smith's mines, on the Birmingham Mineral railroad, yesterday afternoon made a desperate attempt to lynch five white men composing the crew of a freight train. The train ran over and killed Clara Dickson, a colored woman, who was lying across the track drunk and asleep. Her body was cut into half a dozen pieces of flesh and bones. The train crew took shovels and dumped the still bleeding flesh of the woman into a ditch by the road. This made the negroes who had witnessed the accident frantic, and they quickly surrounded the train and sent for a rope. All the crew managed to get on the engine, which they stealthily uncoupled from the train, and by pulling the throttle wide open, managed to escape. A shower of bullets was sent after the flying engine, but they did no harm beyond breaking the cab windows.

OVER FIFTY KILLED. Two Sections of a Loaded Excursion Tram Collide on the Way Home.
Wilkesbarre, Pa., Oct. 11.—The latest figures from the Lehigh valley accident gives the killed at fifty-five and forty injured.

The train which was wrecked was a special on the Lehigh Valley road which was returning from Hazeton with the Wilkesbarre delegation to do the Father Matthew celebration. The excursion trains from Luzerne and Lackawanna counties were in seven sections. The fourth section, on the return home, was standing on the track at Mud Run, near Penn house, when the following section swept around a curve and crashed into it. The road at that point runs near the Lehigh river, and several of the broken cars rolled down the embankment and lie close to the water's edge.

Cincinnati, Oct. 14.—A Post special from Wilkesbarre, Penn., says: "The Father Matthew celebration at Hazelton yesterday ended in a most frightful disaster, the like of which has never been seen before on the Lehigh Valley railroad, or indeed in this country. The wreck occurred at Mud Run, about midway between White Haven and Penn Haven Junction. The first section, while standing still, was run into by the second section. The last three cars of the first section, filled to overflowing, were totally wrecked and all the passengers in the rear car were killed. The last two cars were telescoped and the passengers were either crushed to death or pressed against the boiler and burned to death. The scene was heart rending and beggars description. It was nearly six hours afterwards before the first section was able to reach Wilkesbarre, the wounded being conveyed in ambulances from Mill creek to the city hospital. Passengers on several sections of the train tell tales too horrible for belief under any other circumstances. They relate that the third section of the excursion train stood on the track a few hundred yards from Mud Run waiting for the sections ahead to get out of the way. A brakeman, so they said, had been sent back with a lantern to guard the train in therear. Suddenly they saw the train approaching from the rear at a high rate of speed. Several who were on the rear platform jumped off and escaped. One young woman sprang but seeing two little boys who were in her charge yet on the platform, she climbed back to rescue them and lost her life by her daring. In one instant the flash of the headlight illuminated the interior of the ill-fated car, there was a frightful crash and the engine plunged its full length into the crowded mass of humanity. The shock drove the rear car through the next one for two-thirds of its length and the second into the third. It is not likely that a single person escaped in the rear car. The second was crowded with maimed and bleeding bodies and the third car had but few passengers who escaped. The passengers throughout both trains were terribly shaken up and bruised. They soon swarmed upon the track and the full horror of the accident dawned upon them. Throngs from the two trains gathered beside the telescoped engine and car and there witnessed the most fearful sight of their lives. The shattered engine was pouring forth steam and streams of water which partly hid from human eye many horrible sights. The hissing steam deadened the groans of those involved in the ruin. Ghastly white faces peered into windows to be greeted by faces more ghastly, already dead. Gripped in broken timbers some sat erect as life, staring open-eyed as if aware of the horrible surroundings. Here a youth.

A freight train, in charge of Conductor Brantley and his crew, ran over and killed a colored woman named Clara Dickson at Smith's mines, eight miles from this city. The train was stopped and some of the crew took a shovel and threw the fragments of the body from the track. About 200 negro miners had witnessed the accident, and when the crew handle the woman's body in such a manner they became indignant. Many of them were drinking, and nearly all armed. They surrounded the train with their pistols drawn, and swore they would lynch the entire crew. The crew of the train got on the engine, and a brakeman stealthily uncoupled it from the train. Judge Gantt in the Political Campaign.

Judge James B. Gantt, who has received a multitude of invitations to speak this campaign, has thus far been able to fill but very few appointments made for him, on account of sickness in his family.

Though invited also by the state committee to take part in the state campaign, he was unable to accept. However, he informed the committee that he would do what he could in the manner of local work, and expected to make a number of speeches in this section before campaign was over. He also promised a number of his friends in the adjoining and neighboring counties, at their repeated solicitations, that he would try to speak for them during the campaign.

Early in the season his wife took sick, and he has been compelled to disappoint some whom he had partially promised to speak to. In Cass county his friends were preparing for him to speak at Gun City, East Lynn and a number of other places. He has also been earnestly sought to speak at Jerico, Stockton, El Dorado and other points in Cedar; at Cole Camp, Lincoln and other places in Benton; and at some place in Dade county. Besides these, Bates and Henry county have claims to hear one of their most honored excircuit judges.

All of these places, and in addition Colhoun, LaDue, Lewis, Windsor, this county, he desires very much to speak at, but the outlook for his being able do so is quite gloomy.

Judge Gantt was seen by a Democrat reporter to-day, to whom he stated that he had hoped to be able to take an active part in this campaign, and was much disappointed thus far in not being able to do so. He hopes however, that sickness may leave his home, and he may yet be able to respond to the call of his numerous friends. Clinton also would like to have an address from him.—Clinton Democrat.

SENATOR W. E. CHANDLER, the brave young hero of New Hampshire, is making a vigorous fight in the defence of the Afro-American in those barbarous counties of the bloody South which will add a star to his that will live from generation to generation. We command Senator Chandler to the highest, as a spirited young champion of equal rights and moral law.

News is received of the killing of two Negros by a mob at Sylvarenas, jail in Smith county Miss., last Friday night. Four Negros were arrested for killing a white man named Lee. A mob broke into jail, but were unable to get into the cage where the accused Negros were confined. So they thrust their guns through the bars and shot two of the prisoners to death. Now will you swallow that, and vote for Cleveland and Democracy this fall?

We learn that some of our good envious harted people are circulating and persuading others to not support this paper, as it is a Democratic Journal. We just want to find out the names of these traitors, for we want to show them something. We defy any man woman or child to show where the AD VOCATE has ever appraised the cause of Democracy or to mislead its people. The ADVOCATE will give a reward to any person that can lead us to the person or persons who has tried to slander us.

We are very indignent over the improper prejudice shown by Mr. Lambon the present manager of the Leavenworth Times in the arrests of the colored and white boys sought stealing papers from his office. We want each and every one of our readers to know just how the colored was treated. Mr. Lambon discovered the two boys taking papers without permission, but was unable to catch the colored boy. He afterward caught him and at once turned him over to the athorities. At the court room Tuesday morning he had the colored boy convicted and the white boy turned aloose, courting him to beware of temptations. Why did he not turn them both loose, if he intended to do so with one? The white boy—as you can see—was as much in fault as the colored lad. It is very natural that he would do all in his power to help his own race; but as we

are all citizens, and are to abide by our own laws, we must be delt accordingly We want Mr. Lambon to destinetly understand that we keep an account of all such dirty tricks as that, and also that he solicites the support of the colored people of this vacinity; and we demand more of him that. The Times has always been the favorite Journal among us, and we are in favor of supporting all good republican Journals; but we do not, and will not under any such circumstances. We are supprised to know that the times has such a man connected; and if SHE means business, let us see it. Bro. Lambon, give an account of your-self?

william-springer-cotton.A1:
MET HIS DUESERTS.
Springer, the Colton Wife-Murderer,
Found Dead.
SAN BERNARDINO, November 7th.—The skeleton of a man was found yesterday about two miles north of town, and it proves to be the remains of the noted murderer, Springer, who murdered his wife at the Transcontinental Hotel at Colton about two years ago. On the remains were found effects of the murdered woman, so that there is no doubt but what it is Springer. The inquest will be held to-morrow.
william-springer-cotton.A2:
SPRINGER'S SKELETON
Supposed to Have been Found Near San Bernardino.
Supposed to Have been Found Near San Bernardino.

The report comes from San Bernardino that the skeleton of a man supposed to have been Springer, who murdered his wife at Colton in January, 1887, had been found in a caffon about eight miles from that place by a party of hunters. The Sheriff went to the spot and found a skeleton attired in a black suit of clothes similar to those which Springer wore. Clasped in the bones of the right hand was a revolver, and through the head over the right ear was a bullet hole. In the pockets of the pants was a plush purse such as was carried by Mrs. Springer, and near the skeleton was found a gold watch known to have belonged to Springer, and another which had belonged to Mrs. Springer. Several other articles of clothing were found near the skeleton which were known to have been the property of the missing man.
william-springer-cotton.A4:
SPRINGER'S BONES.
Their Discovery Revives the Story of His Awful Crime.
Their Discovery Revives the Story of His Awful Crime.

The discovery near Colton of the skeleton of William Springer with evidence of his crime, recalls the incidents which brought him into notice.

On the 28th of December, 1886, William Springer was married to Katherine Handorff at the South Park hotel, on Third street, by Rev. J. M. Buehler of St. Paul's German Lutheran church. The next day the couple took the steamer Los Angeles for San Pedro, and from there went to Colton, where they on Tuesday night put up at the Transcontinental hotel.

As they had not put in an appearance downstairs before noon a chambermaid rapped on their door, and receiving no response opened it with her pass-key. Her eyes rested upon a terrible sight. The nearly nude body of a woman lay upon the bed. One eye and temple had evidently been crushed in with a short-handled hammer, which laid beside her, and her head was almost severed from her shoulders. The baggage had been ransacked, and everything of value except $12 in coin had been taken. A number of papers, her clothing and other things, by which she might have been identified, were piled in the middle of the floor and had been set on fire.

Some unburned photographs and some letters revealed that she had been a comely woman of about 20 years and known as Miss Katie Handorff, of Livermore. The citizens of Colton and San Bernardino were terribly wrought up over the occurrence. They buried the body respectably and set about searching for the murderer, freely talking of lynching Springer if he could be found. Captain Lees and other members of the detective service labored in vain for traces of the fugitive. Several suspicious characters were arrested in various parts of the State, but all were proven innocent.

It was learned that Springer was a native of Neuendick, Germany, and had been in the United States about ten years. He had been known under several aliases, in Tombstone, Ariz., and El Paso, Tex. He at one time had some interest in a Market-street saloon in this city, but afterward kept a disreputable saloon at Lodi, about fourteen miles from Stockton, at the same time residing with a Negro woman, who was afterward driven from the town. His whole history is bad, and only by deception could he have induced a respectable girl to have linked her life with his.

The victim had been a servant-girl in the hotel where she was married. She had saved about $300, and owned some little jewelry, and in all probability it was for this that Springer played the lover and afterwards killed her. Her parents are still living in Germany, and her Uncle, Max Ranke, is a large land owner of Livermore.—[S. F. Call.

william-woods-sherman-1888-06-08.A1:
A BLACK FIEND.
Arrest of a Negro Who Committed an Outrageous Deed at Sherman. Threats of Lynching.
Conjctures as to His Connection With the Murder of Genie Watkins at Gainesville—His History.
Special to the Gazette.

SHERMAN, TEX, June 8.—City Marshal Blaine of this city and Deputy Sheriff Whitesides arrived in the city this evening at 6:30 o'clock from Dallas with a negro by the name of William Woods, charged with an outrage and assault on Mrs. Maggie Miles, a white servant who works for the family of J. R. Cole in this city. The following facts in the case have been fully developed to-day: Mrs. Miles occupied a servant's room in the rear of the residence. The room stands inside of and within two feet of the fence, or an alley, with a window on the side next to the alley. The sash in the window was up, and yesterday morning, about 3 o'clock, Mrs. Miles awoke and found herself firmly clinched in

THE GRASP OF A NEGRO MAN.

He told her that his name was Sam, and that if she made any resistance or screamed he would kill her. She made one effort to disengage herself from him, striking her hand against a sharp knife or razor which he held, and suddenly remembering the fate of Miss Genie Watkins, who was murdered by a demon in the same manner at Gainesville last year, ceased to make any resistance. After performing his brutal deed the black demon quickly made his escape by leaping out of the window. Mrs. Miles positively affirms that the negro William Woods is the one who committed the deed, though he left here for Dallas on Tuesday, and the negroes at the boarding house where he stopped state that he lodged there on the night that the deed was committed. Great excitement prevailed when he was brought to the city this evening and strong fears of lynching were entertained, though the Sheriff carried his prisoner by a circuitous route to the jail under a strong guard, and but few knew that he had arrived until he was locked up; and the strong probability of a proof of an alibi caused the enraged populace to desist until further investigations. There is

A STRANGE CIRCUMSTANCE connected with this affair. Mrs. Miles was in the employ of Mrs. Watkins, at Dallas, when her daughter, Miss Gomee Watkins, was assaulted and murdered by an unknown party while asleep in her house at night, last year, at the residence of the Bostick family at Gainesville. There are various conjectures regarding the whole affair which may yet result in wonderful developments. Mrs. Miles will visit the prison to-morrow for the purpose of identifying the negro, and should he prove guilty lynching will be inevitable.
william-woods-sherman-1888-06-08.A2:
No New Developments in the Outrage Case —Off for the Penitentiary.

Special to the Gazette.

SHERMAN, TEX, June 9 —There have been no new developments in the Mrs. Maggie Miles cutrage case. The negro William Woods is still held in jail and an investigation could not be had to-day as Mrs. Miles is quite ill from the effects of mental excitement and the fright she received when assaulted. She has not been able to see the negro, William Woods, but still contends that he is the one who committed the outrage on her as she knew him well, he having worked as porter at the residence of Sam Lazarus, which is next door to J. R Cole's residence, where Mrs. Miles lives, and where she was assaulted and outraged by a negro day before yesterday morning while asleep in her room. The determination among the people to lynch the negro Woods if guilty of the crime is still strong, though circumstances which appear to establish his innocence cause them to desist, and while it is the general impression that Mrs. Miles will identify Woods as the negro who committed the assault, it is highly probable that an alibi will be proven by a number of witnesses both in Sherman and Dallas. Among those who will appear as Woods' material witnesses is Judge Nat Gunter of this city, who was in Dallas on the night the assault was committed and states that he saw Woods in that city at 9 o'clock that night, which would render it impossible for him to have reached Sherman in time to commit the deed, as there was no train leaving there next morning. Woods is a young negre about twenty-three years of age, is about medium size and quite black, and the theory is that as the night was quite dark and being greatly terrified and excited Mrs. Miles mistook the fiend who assaulted her for Woods, being probably of the same stature and appearance.

william-woods-sherman-1888-06-08.A5:
STATE NEWS.
Reports from Goliad county say the rain of Thursday was a perfect flood.
At a depth of 185 feet a large stream of pure water is struck at Washburne.
Another Bean has arrived at Bonham, this time from Dade county, Mo.
At Temple, a young lawyer, named Harry Waters, is arrested for stealing.
Judge Maltbie's remains are forwarded from Austin to McKinney, for burial.
Many people are attending the reunion of the war veterans encamped at Malikoff.
Bee county contemplates getting up a nice exhibit for the San Antonio and Dallas fairs.
Copious rains have fallen around Victoria in the past few days, with prospects of more.
The Tylerites return home jubilant over the victory won by them over the Palestine ball club.

The annual shoot and ball of the New Braunfels Schuetzen Verein, on the 4th, was a success.

Mr. John J. Hand, formerly one of the proprietors of the Galveston News, is lying dangerously ill.

An old Mexican war veteran is sentenced to five years imprisonment for horse theft at McKinney.

The Eagle Pass nine return from Uvalde feeling very blue, having been beaten by a score of 10 to 6.

Fred Von Detwel, dies at Paris from taking five grains of morphine.

The suit against the Texas Pan-electric Telephone Co., by the American Bell Telephone Co., is ended.

Bonham is making preparations for the entertainment of the ex-confederates and G. A. R. posts on August 2.
Dr. Wallace, superintendent of the Terrell asylum is in Austin to arrange the plans for additions to the buildings.

There is strong probability of a large wholesale house being established in Eagle Pass by a firm experienced in frontier business.

Some of the young ladies of Laredo have been circulating a subscription list for the benefit of the flood sufferers at Leon, Mex.

The trial of the negro Carson, for outraging Mrs. Maggie Miles, is going on at Sherman. There are important witnesses on both sides.

The summer normal school opened at Calvert last Monday morning with 36 in attendance, and more teachers coming in on every train.

John Gray, alias Long John, the San Angelo and Ballinger stage robber, is now languishing in the county jail under various indictments.

W. K. Weaver, a press feeder at the Dallas Lithograph company's establishment, has his arm caught, while oiling one of the large presses, and was frightfully lacerated.

Immigration work goes on quietly, but actively at the office of the State Bureau of Immigration. Col. Chilton, chief of the Bureau, finds it necessary to move into a larger building.

Fire broke out in the general freight office of the Southern Pacific at Houston, and though little damage was done by the flames, the water did a great deal of injury to the valuable books and records of the company.

The Postmaster of Hempstead finds 250 printed circulars, postage paid, addressed to persons in that place, also one to himself. As the contents are a review of all the crimes in Waller county for many years, and make pointed charges against one of the prominent citizens there, the Postmaster, before delivering them, has laid the matter before the U. S. district attorney.
